articles.title: No. 5 Michigan tops No. 2 UConn and coach Kim Barnes Arico ends another Geno Auriemma winning streak
articles.content: ANN ARBOR (AP) — Kim Barnes Arico has steadily built the Michigan women’s basketball program into a power. And now in her 15th season, the Wolverines have a signature win. Te’Yala Delfosse scored a career-high 22 points and Olivia Olson had 19 points, lifting No. 5 Michigan to a 77-66 win over No. 2 Connecticut on Thursday night in the first matchup of top-five women’s basketball teams in the AP Top 25 at Crisler Center. “How many teams beat UConn? It doesn’t happen,” Barnes Arico said. The Huskies had won 39 regular-season games in a row since their last loss on Feb. 6, 2025. It wasn’t the first time they ended a long winning streak against Barnes Arico. In her last season at St. John’s, she helped the Red Storm end UConn’s 99-game home winning streak in 2012. “To have UConn come here and be able to knock off the best team in college basketball, or one of the best teams, it is really, really cool,” she said. “I’m happy for our players and our fans.” After the final buzzer, hundreds of the 9,575 fans at the game flooded the floor to celebrate with the team. “This was really special,” Barnes Arico said. “I think it’s great for Michigan, and great for Michigan women’s basketball.” After three closely contested quarters, the Wolverines pulled away early in the fourth quarter and held on for the win. “Michigan was way more ready from the opening tip for this game than we were,” UConn coach Geno Auriemma said. “They were better organized, they were more discipline, they ran their stuff. “It was disappointing, more than anything.” Auriemma, though, knows his team lost to a team that may end up being a contender under Barnes Arico. “They have a really good team,” he said. “It’s one game for them, but they’ve put themselves in a position to say, ‘Why can’t we be a Final Four team?’ “That certainly wasn’t the case 10 years ago so all the credit to her and her staff.” Barnes Arico is quick to redirect credit to her players. Her deep and balanced roster is led by a group of juniors, including Olson, a third-team, All-America forward, and 2024 Olympian Syla Swords, who bought into Barnes Arico’s vision of turning Michigan into one of the best programs in college basketball. “It’s why we came here,” Olson said. “We had belief in coach and we had belief in the program and we wanted to build it to a place it hasn’t been.”

Progress for children in Serbia remains uneven, with inequalities persisting
articles.content: New MICS 7 findings highlight gains in some areas, stalled progress in others and emerging challenges Belgrade, 5 November 2026 – Serbia has made progress in improving the lives of children and families, with improvements in preschool attendance and early initiation of breastfeeding. However, significant inequalities persist, particularly among the poorest and most disadvantaged households, while progress has stalled in areas such as violent disciplining of children, according to findings from the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS 7), released today. Conducted by the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia, with leadership support from the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and in collaboration with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the surveys provide the most comprehensive single source of data on the situation of women and children in Serbia. They also shed light on emerging challenges, including energy poverty, food insecurity and the mental health of adolescents and young people. “The results presented today are extremely important for evidence-based policymaking and for monitoring the implementation of national and international policies and strategies. MICS also provides data for monitoring 26 Sustainable Development Goal indicators, four of which are being measured through MICS for the first time,” said Branko Josipović, Acting Director of the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia. While national indicators point to improvements in several areas, significant disparities remain between the wealthiest and poorest households, urban and rural communities, and the general population and those living in Roma settlements. These gaps are particularly concerning in areas such as child protection, health and equitable access to essential services. “Serbia has made important progress for children, but the new findings show that significant challenges and inequalities remain. MICS allows us to look beyond national averages and see which children are being left behind, and where. The findings point to three clear priorities: investing earlier in children's lives, before disadvantages become entrenched; directing more support to those facing the greatest barriers; and ensuring that education, health, social protection and child protection services work together to meet the needs of children and families. We now have the evidence. Our responsibility is to turn it into action and measurable improvements in children's lives,” said Christina de Bruin, UNICEF Representative in Serbia. The survey also covers a broad range of social and demographic indicators, providing a comprehensive picture of the situation in Serbia. “The MICS 7 findings also highlight the importance of continued investment in sexual and reproductive health, education and economic opportunities for women and young people. It is particularly important that every woman and young person has access to the information and services they need to make informed decisions about their health, lives and futures. This is essential not only for the realisation of individual rights and potential, but also for long-term demographic resilience and the development of society as a whole,” said Borka Jeremić, Head of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Office in Serbia. The MICS findings come at an important moment for Serbia, providing a strong evidence base to inform priorities, policies and investments in the years ahead. They offer an opportunity to put children, particularly those facing the greatest disadvantages, at the centre of decisions about the country's future. The value of MICS 7 is to guide decisions in health, education, social protection and child protection, as well as efforts to address emerging challenges such as energy poverty and mental health. The findings will also support the monitoring of national strategies and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. Serbia is making progress in many areas for children. Findings from the MICS survey confirm near-universal coverage in terms of health insurance and primary education. Progress has also been achieved in preschool education and the early initiation of breastfeeding, while school completion rates across the general population remain high. Preschool enrolment rates (for children aged 36–59 months) have increased across all groups; however, they remain below both national and EU targets, and inequalities persist. 76 percent of children aged 3–4 years now attend preschool programs. Compared to 2019—when 61 percent of children attended preschool—there has been an increase in the share of children from the poorest households and those living in non-urban areas. Nevertheless, further attention must be given to areas where stagnation is observed, such as poverty in rural settings, violent disciplinary practices, immunization, or where backsliding is noted, such as infant mortality within Roma settlements. Poverty is three times more present in rural and semi-urban areas than urban ones. Moderate to severe food insecurity has been experienced by 8 per cent of Serbia’s population, of which 7 per cent is moderate, and 1 per cent severe. In Roma settlements it has been experienced by 52 per cent of the population. Eight per cent of households would like to heat all rooms but cannot afford to, and nine percent would like to cool all rooms but cannot afford to. Ten percent of households have not implemented any energy efficiency measures in the last 15 years. 49 percent of children aged 1 to 14 years of age experience violent disciplining at home, in Roma settlements it is 65 percent. There is stagnation in this area since 2014. In the last 12 months, 18 per cent of women aged 15–49 years have felt discriminated against or harassed on at least one basis. This was most often based on political affiliation (10 per cent). In Roma settlements 13 per cent of women aged 15–49 have felt discriminated against or harassed on at least one basis. This was most often based on ethnic background (7 per cent). In Serbia, 6 per cent of adolescents and youth aged 15–24 reported symptoms of depression or anxiety during the two weeks preceding the survey. Among them, 77 per cent stated that those symptoms led to limitations in daily activities or relationships. In Roma settlements, 14 per cent of adolescents and youth aged 15–24 reported symptoms of depression or anxiety. Backsliding of infant mortality of children in Roma settlements is observed – it has increased to 17 per 1,000 live births (from 8 in 2019), while under-five mortality is 19 per 1,000 live births [SDG 3.2.1], (up from 9 in 2019). Full immunisation coverage of children (24-35 months) is at 79.2 %, roughly the same as in 2019. Full immunisation coverage of children in Roma settlements (24-35 months) is at 56.3%, lower than in 2019 by almost 10 percentage points1. Timeliness of the measles vaccine (by 15 months of age) is 37% in the general population and 27% among children in Roma settlements. Discrepancies are still stark in many areas for poor children, rural children, Roma children and children with functional difficulties. We must continue to make all systems work for all children. The full report of the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS 7) is available HERE. UNICEF works in some of the world’s toughest places, to reach the world’s most disadvantaged children. Across more than 190 countries and territories, we work for every child, everywhere, to build a better world for everyone. Follow UNICEF on Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube

articles.title: Dearborn Public Schools celebrates passage of $1.5 billion bond
articles.description: District leaders say the bond is one of the largest in state history. But they also say it comes after two decades of underspending on school infrastructure.
articles.content: Superintendent Mike Esseily celebrates the passage of a historic infrastructure millage for Dearborn Public Schools at a press conference on November 5, 2026. (Etai Smotrich-Barr / Michigan Public)Dearborn public schools are set to receive significant infrastructure upgrades after voters approved a $1.5 billion millage on Tuesday.District leaders said the bond is one of the largest in state history. But they also said it comes after two decades of underspending on school infrastructure.The money will go towards the construction of six new buildings, as well as major renovations across remaining schools.“Tuesday was a statement about who we are as a community and what we believe our children deserve,” Superintendent Mike Esseily said at a press conference on Thursday. “We are not just building and improving schools. We are building opportunities for generations of children to come.”The work will be completed in four phases across 20 years, with construction beginning on the most urgent priorities next year. As part of the plan, the district will close some aging elementary and middle schools. Students in those areas will attend consolidated facilities serving pre-K through 8th grade. Those new buildings will split elementary and middle school students into separate classroom wings, but will share facilities like gyms, cafeterias, and elective-education classrooms.Esseily said the size of the bond allows the district to make long term plans and avoid “a band-aid approach” to funding infrastructure improvements.“I’m hoping we’re not asking anything of the community for another 50, 60 years,” Esseily said. “We want this bond to last generations of students to come.”District officials say the cost to taxpayers will be offset by reductions in other taxes.Homeowners in the school district, which includes most of Dearborn and a small portion of Dearborn Heights, will be assessed 3.14 mills ($314 for every $100,000 of taxable value) next year for the bond. But the city plans to decrease a sewer-related tax of 0.96 mills and the district will waive an operating millage of 2.18 mills, counterbalancing the increase. As other taxes continue to fall off the books, the city plans to increase its tax assessment for the school bond.In 2019, the district asked voters for a $240 million infrastructure improvement bond. That was only half of what was needed in renovations at the time, according to School Board Trustee Adel Mozip. Voters rejected the proposal by just 242 votes.Following that loss, administrators returned to the drawing board to hear from community members and analyze needs. The result was a proposal six times larger than the last, but one focused on long-term solutions.“Losing [the 2019 millage] was a blessing in a disguise,” Mozip said. “We needed a transformational bond where we actually want to rebuild from the beginning and offer these transformational spaces for our kids.”On Tuesday, the millage passed with 68% of the vote, according to unofficial results released by Wayne County.Don Wotruba, executive director of the Michigan Association of School Boards, said voters often rebuke school millages — especially big ones — if they don’t trust administrators or don’t believe improvements are necessary.But in this case, Wotruba said, the margin of victory suggests that “voters said, ‘I clearly understand what Dearborn is asking for … and if this is what the need is, we're going to support that.”Despite Dearborn’s success, Wotruba said he didn’t expect to see another billion dollar bond on the ballot anytime soon.As much as the eye-popping number is an investment in the future, it’s also a long-awaited supplement to decades of limited spending by Dearborn Public Schools, officials said.“If you go back and look at their previous bond issues,” said Wotruba, “they haven’t done much.”

articles.title: Michigan election watchers celebrate smooth operation in Tuesday's midterms
articles.description: Michigan Election Protection Coalition and local officials are celebrating a successful midterm election, crediting it to the deployment of hundreds of trained volunteers and poll workers.
articles.content: Voters cast ballots in Ypsilanti, Michigan, on November 3, 2026.(Mercedes Mejia / Michigan Public)The nonpartisan Michigan Election Protection Coalition and the American Civil Liberties Union of Michigan are celebrating a successful execution of Tuesday's midterm election in the state.Despite minor tabulator malfunctions, periods of long lines, and a bomb threat at a polling site inside Carlson High School in Gibraltar, organizers said challenges were quickly resolved.Lynna Kaucheck, director of communications for the social justice organization Michigan Voices, highlighted how election workers adapted to the circumstances at the high school."There was almost no interruption in voting. They had generators. They moved everything to the parking lot and people kept voting. And then once the scene was cleared, they moved voting back inside. It was truly incredible," Kaucheck said.The coalition credited the operational success to the training and deployment of hundreds of nonpartisan election challengers, poll workers, and volunteers who helped protect the process across the state.Grand Rapids City Clerk Joel Hondorp noted that his city utilized more than 500 poll workers, 76 of whom he said were brand-new election inspectors."Once again, with the help of the staff, the community all of our election partners, our election ran as it was intended, securely, transparently, smoothly, and with accurate results," Hondorp said.Though Election Day has passed, the coalition said its work is not finished.Jessica Ayoub, deputy political director at the ACLU of Michigan, said organizers were phone banking to help voters fix curable ballot issues, such as missing signatures, to ensure every eligible vote was counted."To date, over 80% of the voters we've talked to have plans to cure their ballot," Ayoub said.The group was shifting its focus to the post-election process, working to ensure that county boards of canvassers across all 83 counties officially certify the election results. Ayoub emphasized that this step is mandatory under state law."The role of boards of county canvassers is not discretionary. Our state constitution and Michigan election laws state that elections must be certified based only on the official record of votes cast," Ayoub said.Once certification is complete, the coalition plans to turn its attention toward preparing for the next presidential cycle."Together, we sent our message loud and clear," Ayoub concluded. "Elections belong to the people, and we look forward to building on the success of this year's election protection efforts as we turn our attention to the 2028 elections."

articles.title: De La Salle attacking history of possible 3-peat while going up against top-ranked St. Joseph
articles.content: When Warren De La Salle takes the soccer pitch one final time in the 2026 season on Saturday, the Pilots will have a mission. That is to win a rare third straight state champion in the MHSAA’s upper divisions. When combining Class A, Class B, Division 1 and Division 2, no school has ever won three straight state championships in those classes and divisions. “If we can do it, win three straight state championships, it will be the first time it has happened in the upper divisions,” echoed De La Salle coach Thaier Mukhtar. “That just shows that this is not easy. It’s never been done before at this level. We have as good of a chance as anybody.” De La Salle does have a chance at history and is one win from accomplishing that – feat. Birmingham Detroit Country Day – another one of Michigan’s premier all-time boys soccer programs – did capture eight straight state titles from 1987-1994, but those titles were scattered between Class C-D (1987-1990) and Class B (1991-94) and not in one same division. Down in the lower divisions and classes, the 3-peat has occurred. Muskegon Western Michigan Christian won three straight in Division 4 from 2022-2024 – the last team to reach that rare feat – while Allen Park Inter-City Baptist also won three straight state title in Class D from 1983-85 back in the early days of the MHSAA state tournament. Several schools have won two straight state titles, but De La Salle has a shot at becoming just the fourth program since the MHSAA adopted boys soccer in 1982 to win three or more straight state titles in the sport. Even some of the largest state powerhouse programs of all-time, such as Troy Athens and Livonia Stevenson, have never accomplished the feat. Neither has East Kentwood or Grand Rapids Forest Hills Central, Grand Rapids Christian, East Lansing and a host of others over the past 45-plus years. Even in the old Michigan Suburban Coaches Association state tournament (1974-1981) did any school ever win three straight in that tournament that predates the MHSAA state tournament. Playing in its fourth straight Division 2 Final Four this week, De La Salle advanced Wednesday night with a 3-2 victory over DeWitt to reach the state title game for the third straight season. “This has been the goal all along. To be back in the finals and try to win another state championship,” reminded Mukhtar. “I’m happy for the kids because you just never know what could happen.” Although it is of no surprise that the No. 6-ranked and talent-laden Pilots made it back even though the road was not easy, De La Salle may not even be the favorite. Its opponent, top-ranked St. Joseph, is undefeated and untied and takes its impeccable track record into Saturday’s 3:30 p.m. state finals game at Grand Ledge High School with some eye-popping numbers. The Bears, the 1992 Class B state runner-up to one of those powerhouse Detroit Country Day teams, is 23-0-0 and both the regular season and conference tournament champions in the Southwestern Michigan Athletic Conference, which is mostly Division 1 schools ands even boasts 2025 Division 1 state champion and longtime power Portage Central. St. Joseph owns a 100-4 scoring edge this season with a school record 20 shutouts, including 12 straight clean sheets. The Bears have outscored five state tournament foes 19-0 and last gave up a goal back on Sept. 17 during a 4-2 triumph over Division 1 and SMAC foe Battle Creek Lakeview. St. Joseph’s 0.22 goals-against average as a team is the lowest of the eight competing schools at this year’s four MHSAA state finals. De La Salle has again played a treacherous schedule of mostly Division 1 schools including several from the top conferences in the state. The Pilots – who have won seven state championships dating back to 1990 and are making their ninth all-time appearance in a state title game – own a 74-21 scoring edge with 12 shutouts this year despite missing one of their top players except for five early-season games. De La Salle has won six postseason games by a 31-6 margin, even defeating Detroit U-D Jesuit in double overtime 3-2 last week in the regional semifinals and knocking off undefeated Macomb Lutheran North (7-1) in the district finals two weeks ago. So, who really is the favorite in the state title game? De La Salle, which has nine state finals appearances, seven state championships, one state runner-up 14 Final Four appearances and 14 regional trophies, 36 district championships and 17 Catholic High School League Central Division championships, has the tournament experience and pedigree to go up against a team which has not tasted defeat since last season. “I really feel like this is the best two teams. I kind of felt when the tournament began if we could beat U-D in the regional (semifinals) then we would see St. Joseph in the finals and here we are,” noted Mukhtar. “They are talented and so are we. We have who I think will be Mr. Soccer, Andrew Corder, and our goalie Dominic (Baldarotta) is one of the best goalies in the state. And we have a lot of other guys who were here last year. I expect it will be a good game. It’s the state finals and those are usually good games.” De La Salle is used to making runs and Mukhtar has won over 900 games as a coach of Dela Salle and both Fraser’s boys and girls teams and has guided many teams to lengthy state tournament runs. He even led Fraser’s boys team to the D-1 Final Four in 2014 during his six-year stint at that school. “I’ve coached a lot of games and I have enjoyed it all,” smiled Mukhtar. “I’ve been blessed with many great players over the years and it’s exciting what this group has a chance to accomplish. Being to four straight final fours and to our third straight state championship game is truly remarkable because I know how hard it is to win in the tournament. Everything has to go your way.” State titles (7) – 1990, 1992, 1993, 2000, 2005, 2024, 2025 State finals appearances (9) – 1990, 1992, 1993, 1994, 2000, 2005, 2024, 2025, 2026 Final Four appearances (14) – 1984, 1987, 1990, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1997, 2000, 2005, 2011, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 Regional championships (14) – 1984, 1987, 1990, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1997, 2000, 2005, 2011, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 District championships (36) – 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 (most recent) CHSL Tournament championships – 1985, 1987, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1995, 1996, 1998, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2011 CHSL Central Division titles (17) – 1985, 1987, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1995, 1996, 1998, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2011

Michigan Dems choose leaders for new legislative majority; GOP ousts Hall as caucus head
articles.description: Democrats will be running both the Michigan House and Senate after big wins in this year’s election. They chose Rep. Ranjeev Puri as the next Speaker of the House.
articles.content: Democrat Ranjeev Puri, on the cusp of making history as the first South Asian speaker of the Michigan House, speaks with reporters at the state Capitol on Thursday, November 5, 2026.(Colin Jackson / Michigan Public Radio Network )The next class of Michigan lawmakers picked their next legislative leaders Thursday.Democrats will be running both the Michigan House of Representatives and Senate after big wins in this year’s election. The party also kept the governor’s office.In the Senate, unofficial results show Democrats picked up three seats to expand their majority from 20-18 to 23-15.Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) will serve as the next Senate Majority Leader. He said he wants the “most productive session in our lifetimes.”“We have an ability here to find pathways forward on all kinds of new policy ideas. Our goal will be, again, to make sure that we can do big, bold things in this new trifecta,” Camilleri said.He named energy, housing, and medicine affordability as some of his priorities for next term.On the Republican side, Sen. Roger Hauck (R-Mt. Pleasant) will run his caucus as minority leader. He imagines finding common ground with Democrats on issues like education, affordable housing, and lowering the cost of health care.Despite the heavy losses, Hauck still joked with reporters Thursday about each side working through some disorder as members cycle in and out.“There will be chaos with them. There will be chaos with us. Hopefully there will be more chaos with them than us,” Hauck said.Most members of both the Democratic and Republican caucuses will be new to the Senate next term.Down the hall in the Michigan Capitol, the House of Representatives will be flipping to Democratic control next year.House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) will assume the role of speaker. This session, Puri led a relatively fresh caucus that had lost the chamber during the 2024 election.House Speaker Matt Hall during the State of the State Address on February 26, 2025.(Lester Graham / Michigan Public )As of Thursday afternoon, the Associated Press had called 62 out of 110 House races for Democrats. It’ll be a far larger majority than before, when every single Democrat needed to vote yes on a bill for it to pass.Democratic Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson said legislative Democrats should pursue a "bold new agenda." Puri said the bigger majority lets his party “dream bigger.”“I don’t want to spend much time litigating who’s playing in what sport or who’s using which restroom. I’m hoping that we can actually move the needle in talking about meaningful problems and solving meaningful problems to help everyone in Michigan succeed,” Puri told reporters.He’ll be the first person of South Asian heritage to lead either chamber of the Legislature. Despite being American-born to parents from India, Puri wore a hat that read “immigrant” to drive home the significance.House Republicans are switching up their leadership. After two terms running his caucus, in both the minority and majority, Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) lost his bid to stay in charge Thursday.Instead, Republicans went with Rep. Tom Kunse (R-Clare).Aggressive policymaking goals and an antagonistic relationship with Democrats have somewhat defined Hall’s tenure as speaker. Notably, he was a driving force behind a multibillion dollar roads deal that also delayed the Fiscal Year 2025 budget.Kunse said he believes Hall has done great things for the caucus, but believes himself to be the best person to lead it in this moment. He plans to be more collaborative with Democrats.“Democrats are not the enemy. Being 45th in education is the enemy,” Kunse told reporters. “Gas is expensive. Affordability is the issue. So, there are things we’re going to work with Democrats on and there are some things that we’re going to have differences on.”Michigan Public Radio Network's Russ McNamara contributed reporting.

'JD, habibi.' Arabs celebrate El-Sayed's use of a term of affection in his victory speech
articles.content: BEIRUT (AP) — From Michigan to the Middle East, Arabs are celebrating Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate win and delighting in his introduction of Arabic terms like “habibi” and “inshallah” to the American political lexicon. After being the target of Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, the rising political star who will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator has mocked his critics on the right while championing the Palestinian cause and leaning into his faith and Egyptian heritage. “JD, habibi,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech, addressing U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who had warned that the candidate would lead rioters in burning down Detroit. “There is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.” “Habibi” literally translates to “my beloved” and is peppered through Arab pop songs. In everyday speech, it often means “buddy,” “pal,” or “bro.” El-Sayed's supporters have sported shirts reading “Habibi for Abdul.” El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, said his campaign had turned “inshallah” — “God willing” — into “hamdulillah,” which means “thank God.” Arabs thrilled to the gentle ribbing of the vice president, with many posting music video clips featuring “habibi” to social media. It was a rare outpouring of joy in a region traumatized by past and present conflicts — which have also fueled negative stereotypes in the West. One user on X posted a video of Egyptian diva Shireen Abd El-Wahab dancing to one of her most popular songs, joking that El-Sayed would make it the new national anthem. Egyptians are renowned in the Arab world for their sense of humor and are known for cracking jokes in the face of life's difficulties, a spirit that has been popularized in films and by famous comedic actors. Riffing off El-Sayed's victory speech, some shared a meme from an Egyptian film in which a man attends a funeral while high and is unable to stop laughing. “I came here to crack jokes,” read the caption, quoting a line from the film. An Egyptian academic, Khalil al-Anani, praised El-Sayed on X, saying: "'Habibi' is the sweetest word.” He thanked the senator-elect for bringing joy to Egyptians. Arab and Muslim Americans have faced prejudice for decades, with popular films depicting them as terrorists and politicians on the right fanning baseless fears about the imposition of sharia, or Islamic law. During the campaign, U.S. President Donald Trump referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist,” evoked the Sept. 11 attacks and deliberately misstated the candidate's name. On social media, users responded to such attacks by posting light-hearted videos, including of Lebanese diva Haifa Wehbe belly dancing and young veiled women breakdancing in the streets. “Donald, look, I know you've struggled with my name,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech. “So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me ‘senator.'” Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. articles.title: Consumers and DTE sue to block "Money out of Politics" proposal
articles.description: Consumers Energy and DTE Energy filed a lawsuit in federal court on Thursday seeking a finding that Proposal 2, Money Out of Politics, is unconstitutional, and blocking it from taking effect.
articles.content: "Many Detroiters were leaving money on the table," said Priscilla Perkins, the President and CEO of the Accounting Aid Society. (Steve Carmody / Michigan Radio)Consumers Energy and DTE Energy filed a lawsuit in federal court Thursday that seeks to block Proposal 2, backed by a group called Michiganders for Money out of Politics, from going into effect.Voters approved the amendment to the Michigan Campaign Finance Act by an overwhelming majority — 81% of voters in unofficial results — on Tuesday.It would ban regulated utilities including DTE Energy and Consumers Energy from making campaign contributions to the governor, attorney general, or a state senator or representative or a candidate for those offices. Employees and relatives of employees of the utilities would also not be permitted to make the campaign contributions.In a statement, Consumers' Director of Media Relations Katie Carey said: "This proposal unfairly targets a Michigan business, its Michigan employees and their family members from exercising their constitutionally protected rights to participate in the political process, while allowing out of state special interest groups and billionaires to continue flooding Michigan with political spending. Michiganders should not lose their First Amendment rights because of where they work."The lawsuit said the measure violates the First Amendment because "it is not directed toward preventing quid pro quo corruption or its appearance and is not closely drawn to that interest.""Lacking any evidence of quid pro quo corruption, the MMOP Initiative offered only slogans and generic references to 'corruption,' 'legalized corruption,' 'pay-to-play politics,' 'big money,' 'special interests,' and 'corporate influence.' Those buzzwords are no substitute for evidence; the government 'must do more than merely recite a general interest in preventing corruption,'" the lawsuit said.The lawsuit names as defendants Jonathan Brater, director of the Michigan Bureau of Elections, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson or her successor in office. (Benson is governor-elect and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist is secretary of state-elect.)The lawsuit seeks a finding that the measure violates the First and Fourteenth amendment rights of the plaintiffs, and a preliminary and permanent injunction of any state effort to investigate violations of the measure and assess fines.Maura Cowley, campaign manager for the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, said in a statement:“This lawsuit is no surprise. The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before. On Tuesday, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people. The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this challenge.”The lawsuit follows one filed on Wednesday by the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a libertarian think tank. That lawsuit sought to challenge only some portions of the proposal.Editor's note: Consumers Energy is among Michigan Public's corporate sponsors.

Puri elected House Speaker as Democrats prepare to take control of state government
articles.description: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri of Canton will lead Michigan’s newly elected Democratic House majority as speaker in January, while Republicans chose state Rep. Tom Kunse of Clare to lead their caucus in the minority, marking a new chapter for both parties as Democrats prepare to take control of state government. The respective caucuses in the […]
articles.content: Michigan House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) walks the Michigan House chamber floor on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Lansing, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)State Rep. Ranjeev Puri of Canton will lead Michigan’s newly elected Democratic House majority as speaker in January, while Republicans chose state Rep. Tom Kunse of Clare to lead their caucus in the minority, marking a new chapter for both parties as Democrats prepare to take control of state government. The respective caucuses in the House held their leadership votes on Thursday following a short session day where attendance was taken but no other voting occurred — aside from the leadership elections taking place behind closed doors. Puri spoke to members of the capitol press corps outside the chamber, and described the last two years as House minority leader as “the most grueling two years of my life.” His caucus retaking control of the House was the result, Puri said, of traveling around the state and making the case that a change was needed in state government. Those efforts bore fruit in Tuesday’s midterm election, giving Puri and his colleagues what he called “a resounding mandate” for more “stable leadership and prioritizing the needs of Michigan.” “We’re ready to do that,” Puri said, adding that he was willing to work with Kunse and anyone, really, who is willing to work with his caucus. Still, he reflected on his past relationship with current House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), as well as the slings and arrows that he had to dodge from the brash and aggressive style of Hall’s leadership. “The last two years have been led with political divisiveness, and every aspect of it seemed to be on how we could own the other side or win a political point,” Puri said. “In my opinion, that’s not how this institution was designed to run, and so the House Democrats are focused on ‘Team Michigan’ and making sure that we’re making the lives of everyday Michiganders easier and better.” Michigan House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to members of the news media on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, outside of the House chamber in Lansing, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Puri added that if they had partners on the other side of the aisle, who are willing to put politics aside, they can move forward on that goal. “The needs of Michigan are transformative, and we need to think about how we tackle systemic issues that are plaguing our state,” he said. “Median household incomes are lagging behind some of our peer states. We still are not seeing population growth in the way that we want. So I’m hoping, with the size of the majority, that we’re able to tackle real issues.” One thing that Puri doesn’t want to spend time on is litigating culture war issues like “who’s playing in what sport, or who’s going to use which restroom.” “I’m hopeful that there was some semblance of understanding with the leadership change in the other caucus that maybe that approach wasn’t working,” he said. In that vein, Puri said he also hoped that the election brought a new set of core values to the House, and that it would have the potential to move the state’s politics “in a direction that is more fair.” In choosing Kunse, House GOP will try a new approach to working with Dems Although all eyes were on the Democrats after they secured another government trifecta in the 2026 elections — nabbing the governor’s office, the other two executive branch offices, control of the Legislature and near complete control of the Michigan Supreme Court — the leadership battle on the GOP side of the chamber was of high import. Hall led the caucus through its minority leader position during the 2023-24 session, in which the Democrats also held a government trifecta, and into the 2025-26 session, where he served at top of the caucus as speaker. Hall had said before the elections that his caucus would work hard to retain its majority in the House, even if the Senate Democrats were able to retain theirs, and that he could do that all in the face of a highly-favorable Democratic year. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE A blue wave, however, swept the nation and Michigan on Tuesday, and that pushed out several key members of the GOP House caucus. Hall faced a serious challenge for his own seat, but prevailed, albeit narrowly, against House District 42 Democratic nominee Nick Rowe, winning only by 3.2 percentage points. While Republicans chose to move on from Hall’s leadership on Thursday, the speaker will be remembered for his brash and aggressive approach to commanding power in the House, as he routinely mocked his House Democratic colleagues from the bully pulpit of his own press conferences. Hall also dared Democrats to blink on all manner of policy points and budget fights over his two years of leading the caucus. In some respects, Hall was successful in doing the latter, especially during the 2025 budget fight. Kunse thanked Hall for his leadership over the last few years, but said he would do things a bit differently. “We’re going to do better, and what we’re going to do is show the state of Michigan, number one, that we care,” Kunse said. “We understand that things are expensive, and we understand that education needs to be addressed.” State Rep. Tom Kunse (R-Clare) speaks to members of the capitol press corps after being an elected Michigan House minority leader on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Lansing, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Kunse said Hall did some good things for the caucus and that there were indeed times when the GOP needed to stand up and say, “No, this is bad policy.” “I commend him on that,” Kunse said, while also making it clear that he would not blame Hall or any other GOP member for the loss of 11 seats in the 2026 election. “I have nothing but respect for Matt Hall.” In a break from Hall’s harsh rhetoric, Kunse said his minority leadership in the House would commence with a guiding ethos that “Democrats are not the enemy.” “Being 45th in education is the enemy,” Kunse added. “Affordability is the issue. There are things that we’re going to work with Democrats on, and there are some things we’re going to have differences on. But what I’m excited about with the team is the professionalism.” There were many times when Hall used his position as speaker to go after Puri, as well as Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, in a head-on and sometimes personal way. Michigan House speaker refuses to reinstate Democratic legislator to Appropriations Committee role Kunse said the media and the residents of the state won’t be seeing or reading about “our differences on Facebook because we’re going to go into the office and we’re going to say, ‘Listen, we’re not there today, we have a difference of opinion on this.’” On the House losing its majority, Kunse recognized that they “lost some good people,” but also that “politics is a blood sport.” “Some of my friends aren’t here anymore,” Kunse said. “I’m sad, I’m angry. I don’t think finding blame is what’s going to be productive. Gov. Snyder had ‘positive, relentless action,’ right? I’m totally stealing that from him. To me, that’s better. Let’s move forward. What are we going to do to get this problem solved? What are we going to do to get back the majority? I don’t have any interest in assigning blame.” Puri, Kunse give an early look into the priorities of both caucuses The respective leaders in the House said they are still getting their ducks in a row, meeting their new members and devising battle plans for the road ahead. Puri’s majority caucus will focus its efforts this year on affordability, household incomes, population growth and the systemic issues that appear to be holding Michigan back. Puri raised utility costs as an area of concern regarding affordability. Whereas the previous 2023-24 Democratic trifecta that had pushed a large amount of legislation swiftly, Puri said Thursday that “the question is, how do you measure productivity?” “I think at times, sometimes it’s on the quantity of how many public acts have been passed, but for me, it’s the impact of the bills that we do,” he said. “There are a number of systemic issues that we can be thinking about and deliberating on what to do.” Kunse was asked the same question, and landed on it in the same way that Puri did — those plans will come with time. “Our team has been together for 33 minutes,” Kunse said. “We are working on that. Do I have a detailed plan? No, but I can tell you that education is not acceptable where it’s at. We need to talk about healthcare. The pricing of healthcare is not acceptable. I can’t tell you how we’re going to do it, but I can tell you that these are things that we want to do.” Detroit Caucus elects new executive board members New members of the House Detroit Caucus were also elected on Thursday. State Rep. Stephanie Young will again serve as the caucus chair, and state Rep. Tonya Myers Phillips will serve as its vice chair. “We are experiencing the dangerous policies from the White House through cuts to Medicaid and SNAP and exorbitant grocery and gasoline prices,” Young said in a statement. “My colleagues and I are laser focused on policies to reverse these devastating decisions and usher in a better Detroit for all of us. I am especially grateful for the team of Detroiters assembled to lead the Detroit Caucus and value our collective voice for positive change over the next two years.”

articles.title: Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law
articles.description: If it goes into effect next year, this California law would restrict social media access for children under 16.
articles.content: Meta, Google, and TikTok have each filed lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta in an attempt to block a law that restricts social media features it deems addictive for users under 16. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill, known as AB 1709, into law in September, and it’s slated to take effect at the start of the new year. The law prohibits social platforms from offering autoplay videos and personalized feeds to users under 16, and it requires the platforms to delete these users’ accounts if they don’t turn those features off. If platforms do not comply, they could be liable for fines of up to $50,000 per affected user under 16 years old. Meta claims that AB 1709 violates the First Amendment by overriding its editorial decisions about how to display content, adding that Section 230 preempts the law. TikTok and Google made similar arguments. “Meta currently organizes its feeds of content to include personalized content recommendations and to automatically play media, [so] the Act would make it unlawful for Meta to disseminate speech to minors altogether, and would require Meta to delete minors’ accounts, unless it changes these practices,” the company wrote in its lawsuit. In an emailed statement, a TikTok spokesperson added, “AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use.” AB 1709 follows a trend of legislation around the world that seeks to curb teen social media use in an attempt to improve teen mental health outcomes. However, digital safety experts often caution against these laws because they can inadvertently compromise the privacy of all platform users, including adults, by requiring age verification checks that collect more user data. “AB 1709 compels platforms to collect even more information from every user, invading everyone’s privacy and frustrating our ability to remain anonymous online,” EFF Associate Director of State Affairs Rindala Alajaji said in a press briefing. “Online surveillance by social media companies is harmful, and yet this bill requires even more of it, further concentrating power in the hands of tech companies rather than actually protecting users.” Alajaji added that teenagers’ use of social media has been instrumental in enabling impactful digital activism, citing the Parkland shooting survivors’ March for Our Lives and climate activist Greta Thunberg’s global reach. “As a functional ban on social media for youth under 16, AB 1709 cuts young people off from essential information and experiences, silencing the very voices it claims to protect,” Alajaji said. These platforms are primed to fight this California law as they navigate similar legal battles in various countries. That’s especially true for Meta, which agreed to pay a settlement of up to $18 billion to resolve children’s safety claims brought by 29 U.S. states. In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban social media for users under 16 altogether. France passed a similar law, but its top court struck it down, citing concerns about violations of free expression rights. These platforms also argue that the law would affect parents’ ability to make decisions about their teens’ internet use through parental controls. A Google spokesperson noted that autoplay on YouTube is turned off for minors by default, and that parents have the ability to turn off their teens’ access to Shorts altogether. “We believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,” a Google spokesperson said. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.” A representative for Attorney General Bonta said that his office is reviewing the filings and is committed to “defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. Trump, who tore down the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom, said “no major modifications” should be made to those rooms without the approval of Congress. “We’ve had a lot of victories in this office,” Trump said. “So we’re making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people.” After this week’s midterm elections, in which Republicans lost majorities in both chambers of Congress, the president has focused on renovation projects across Washington, D.C. The day after Republicans’ devastating losses across the country, his post-election press conference focused on updates about the construction of the ballroom. Trump said he would ask Congress to codify his executive order. If lawmakers do not do so during the lame-duck session, it’s unlikely to happen in the next Congress with Democrats in charge of both chambers. articles.title: Trump’s gerrymandering push flops as Democrats win redrawn seats
articles.description: Alabama Republicans had hoped Rep. Shomari Figures would deliver a concession speech on Tuesday night after the state legislature redrew his district to be more GOP-friendly. Instead, the Democrat declared victory — winning nearly 54% of the vote. “We know what happened with this district,” Figures told supporters as he invoked the Republican gerrymander. “But […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., speaks at a final rally before the 2026 midterm elections at the Oliver-Dunn Acadome at Alabama State University in Montgomery on Nov. 2, 2026. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Republicans had hoped Rep. Shomari Figures would deliver a concession speech on Tuesday night after the state legislature redrew his district to be more GOP-friendly. Instead, the Democrat declared victory — winning nearly 54% of the vote. “We know what happened with this district,” Figures told supporters as he invoked the Republican gerrymander. “But we had a job to do. And so we put our hands to the plow and we did not look backwards.” The Republican project to gerrymander congressional districts across the country, initiated by President Donald Trump more than a year ago, failed to deliver significant wins for the party — and, in North Carolina at least, even worked against it. Amid a nationwide blue tsunami and voter backlash in Southern states that split apart districts where a majority of residents are Black, Democrats won seats that Republicans redrew to give themselves an advantage. States typically draw new maps every 10 years after the census. But Trump’s redistricting push, which kicked off in Texas in the summer of 2025, triggered a nationwide rush as Republican and Democratic states battled to set the electoral landscape ahead of this week’s midterms. A late April decision from the U.S. Supreme Court set off another round of gerrymanders. The court sharply curtailed federal protections against racial gerrymandering, clearing the way for Southern states to break apart majority-Black districts that often elect Democrats. Republicans had once hoped mid-decade redistricting would create a buffer against the losses the president’s party traditionally suffers in midterm elections. Perhaps, the thinking among Republicans went in 2025, the party could even maintain a narrow majority with the help of the gerrymandered districts. It didn’t turn out that way, as the GOP’s effort proved woefully insufficient against the strength of the Democratic vote. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had won 247 House seats, far above the 218 needed for a majority, while Republicans had won 153, according to The Associated Press. Thirty-five races had yet to be called. “Let this be a lesson: never capitulate, never acquiesce to those who would use power for improper purposes,” Eric Holder, a former U.S. attorney general under President Barack Obama and the chairman of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in a statement. Gains were expected New Republican maps could have netted the party as many as 15 seats, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter. GOP-controlled state legislatures advanced news maps in Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee, in addition to Alabama and Texas. In response, Democrats successfully gerrymandered a single state, California, where the party picked up five seats it had targeted. Voters approved a Democratic gerrymander in Virginia, but the state Supreme Court struck down the measure. A state court also imposed a Democratic-leaning district in Utah. In states where Republicans targeted Democratic seats for gerrymandering, the party made no net gains, according to a Wednesday memo from the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. “This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, said at a news conference Wednesday as he broadly described his party’s losses. GOP efforts fail DeSantis signed a new Florida map aimed at securing four new GOP seats into law in May. Democrats now appear likely to retain all four. First-time voter Letrice Felton, 50, said she cast a ballot Tuesday at Edgecombe Community College in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, because of rising costs and the state of poverty in her city. (Photo by Elisha Brown/Stateline) The redistricting failure was starkest in North Carolina, where Republicans are on track to lose six seats. In the state’s 1st Congressional District, Democratic Rep. Don Davis won reelection Tuesday with just over 50% of the vote, overcoming a GOP gerrymander in what was the most expensive U.S. House race in history. In Rocky Mount, a city of about 55,000 in North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, Letrice Felton voted for the first time on Tuesday. The 50-year-old said she cast a ballot because of rising costs and poverty within the city. More than 60% of the city’s residents are Black and roughly 1 in 5 residents live in poverty, nearly double the national rate. “To see people out in Rocky Mount, walking with beds of carts, with clothes and stuff,” Felton said. “It’s very sad. And they need help, and it’s like, there’s no resources here for it.” Jislem Rodriguez, 18, voted for the first time Tuesday at Edgecombe Community College in Rocky Mount. Rodriguez said she is concerned about the economy. “Money isn’t really lasting like it used to,” she said. In Texas, state lawmakers sought to secure five additional seats for Republicans. The party instead flipped only a single newly gerrymandered district and suffered a net loss of one seat. Jislem Rodriguez, 18, also voted for the first time Tuesday at Edgecombe Community College and cited the economy as a major concern. (Photo by Elisha Brown/Stateline) When Republicans redrew most of the targeted districts, they assumed Latino voters would continue backing GOP candidates, Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston, said in an interview. A significant share of Latino voters instead cast ballots for Democrats. Nineteen percent of Latino voters in Texas who said they voted for Trump in 2024 voted for Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, in 2026, according to CNN voter polls (poll results weren’t available for specific House races). “On paper, these districts are still Republican but the trend has been in general toward the Republicans and the Latino vote — which these are premised on — has shifted back to the Democrats,” Rottinghaus said. Black voter backlash The NAACP reported strong turnout among Black voters on Tuesday. Eighty-one percent of Black voters supported Democrats in the election, up from 70% in 2024 and 73% in 2022, according to exit poll data analyzed by NPR. Janai Nelson, president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund, a legal advocacy group focused on racial justice, said in a statement that Black turnout was especially pronounced in states that redrew maps following the Supreme Court’s decision on racial gerrymandering — Alabama, Florida, Louisiana and Tennessee. In the case, Louisiana v. Callais, the court’s conservative majority significantly limited the consideration of race when drawing legislative maps. Section 2 of the federal Voting Rights Act had previously limited states from using maps that diluted the voting power of minority citizens. “Black and brown voters made a statement last night,” Nelson said. “Despite relentless attempts to silence their voices and stifle their power, voters of color turned out in extraordinary numbers.” For example, Alabama voter turnout was nearly 44%, up from nearly 39% in 2022. In Montgomery County, part of Figures’ gerrymandered district, turnout among Democratic voters rose 39% over 2022. “I’m at a loss for words, because we had the deck stacked against us,” Figures said during his victory speech. Future maps? The prospects of additional gerrymanders before the 2028 election are mixed. Maryland voters approved a measure that would ease the way for the blue state to pass a Democratic gerrymander. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said Wednesday that he wants new maps after the redistricting measure, called Question 3, passed with 60% of the vote. “Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states,” Moore told reporters Wednesday. The White House didn’t respond to questions about Trump’s support for future GOP redistricting efforts. At least some Republicans have expressed reservations about pursuing new maps after such a sharp rebuke by voters. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican, announced Wednesday that he wouldn’t call the state legislature into special session to pass new maps before the Democratic governor-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms, takes office in January. Kemp had previously called a special session earlier this year, but lawmakers opted not to advance redistricting legislation. “The voters of our state have spoken,” Kemp said in a statement. Gerrymandering critics have called for a national ban on the practice — or at the very least, a ban on the mid-decade redraws. Common Cause, a nonpartisan watchdog that opposes gerrymandering, said the failure of Trump’s redistricting push sets the stage for federal reform. “At the end of the day, the American people this time around, they rejected the attempts to rig the midterms through gerrymandering,” Common Cause president and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón told reporters on Wednesday. In Missouri, voters rejected a gerrymander passed by the GOP-controlled state legislature — called the Missouri First map — that targeted a seat in Kansas City held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. The measure failed resoundingly, 62% to 38%. The map wasn’t in effect for the 2026 election because of a state Supreme Court decision, but voter approval would have implemented it for the 2028 election. “In the future, I hope that the people of Missouri will be served by a Congressional map like the Missouri First map that better represents our state,” Rick Brattin, Cleaver’s Republican opponent, said in a statement that attacked the Missouri Supreme Court for issuing a decision “to benefit Democrats” by blocking the map. Cleaver, who won reelection with 69% of the vote, said in his own statement that his campaign overcame major hurdles, including the gerrymandered map, which was in place for the primary election and part of the general election. “As I’ve always said from the beginning,” Cleaver said, “the will of the people always prevails in the end.” Stateline’s Elisha Brown contributed reporting.

articles.title: Democrats romped in state elections. What will they do with their newfound power?
articles.description: The blue wave that swept across Tuesday’s midterm election will deliver Democrats new power over state government, giving them the opportunity to advance long-sought policy changes. Democrats flipped hundreds of seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Democratic lawmakers from […]
articles.content: Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcom Kenyatta, a Democrat, speaks Wednesday at a party celebrating Democratic control of state government in Harrisburg. Across the country, Democrats flipped hundreds of state legislative seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The blue wave that swept across Tuesday’s midterm election will deliver Democrats new power over state government, giving them the opportunity to advance long-sought policy changes. Democrats flipped hundreds of seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Democratic lawmakers from multiple states pledged to use their new statehouse power to attack rising prices, protect reproductive rights, pass new gun safety measures and grow the housing supply. The changed landscape also gives state Democratic leaders more power to oppose the agenda of President Donald Trump, said Marc Farinella, senior advisor to the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy. That may mean opposing Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts, Farinella said, or bolstering state funding of Medicaid and food stamps, both of which have faced significant federal cuts under Trump. Legislating will prove much easier in states with newly won Democratic trifectas, where the party controls both chambers and the governor’s office. Those states include Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. But newly divided governments in other states — Iowa, Ohio, Georgia, Texas — could result in gridlock. Following the midterms, state legislatures will see their biggest leadership shakeup in years, as the National Conference of State Legislatures expects nearly half of state chambers to have new leaders next session. “None of us have ever been in a majority, so it’s a big learning curve,” said Arizona state Rep. Nancy Gutierrez, assistant House minority leader. She said Democrats, who will control Phoenix for the first time in 60 years, are connecting with their counterparts from other states, such as Colorado, that have swung from red to blue. The Pennsylvania state Senate flipped to Democratic control for the first time since 1978, handing the party a resounding trifecta after Gov. Josh Shapiro sailed to reelection. Already, Shapiro and Democratic state lawmakers have pledged to revive a slew of policies that had previously passed the state House but died in the Republican-controlled Senate. Those include raising the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour, codifying abortion rights, passing a law to allow survivors of sexual abuse to sue their abusers and increasing funding for mass transit. “I think here in Pennsylvania we made very, very clear at the state level and the federal level that we are rejecting Donald Trump’s policies and we want to see costs come down,” Shapiro said Wednesday. “And now you’ve got an opportunity to see that happen in Harrisburg and in Washington.” At the same time, Farinella said, this week’s “historically forceful rebuke of Trump and his agenda” will prompt an as yet undetermined response from Republicans. After a decade of near-total control by Trump and the MAGA movement, the decisive GOP losses could free some Republicans to return to more centrist policies, he said. “To me, it’s the big outstanding question coming out of the election,” Farinella said. “How will the congressional Republicans and how will the Republicans in state legislatures now feel about the latitude they have or don’t have in terms of their own policy preferences?” Progress or gridlock? In New Hampshire, Democrats pulled off a stunning upset, flipping control of both the state House and Senate. Though Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte won reelection, Democrats appear to have secured veto-proof supermajorities. Democratic state Rep. Christal Lloyd said she plans to focus on addressing federal cuts to Medicaid through state funding and address education funding to help alleviate growing local property tax burdens. But she said Democrats won’t just rush to push through progressive bills. “We want to make lasting changes, positive changes, and we want to write good legislation that helps our constituents and helps their lives,” Lloyd told Stateline. “And it’s up to us to live up to the trust that the voters put in our hands.” While the governor won her race, her power will be greatly diminished by legislative supermajorities. “If she tries to veto anything, we’ve got the supermajority,” Lloyd said. “But that’s not to say we won’t work with the other side. We’re going to negotiate where possible.” Democrats will also wield new power in Concord after winning total control of the state executive committee, a unique-to-New-Hampshire body that serves as a check on the governor, approving or rejecting state contracts and vetting gubernatorial nominees. That body has pledged to immediately focus on funding Planned Parenthood and holding the scandal-ridden state Supreme Court accountable. “There is no rubber stamp for the governor,” said state Rep. Luz Bay, a Democrat newly elected to the council. In other states, the new legislative mix may produce gridlock. In North Carolina, Democrats already controlled the governor’s office and on Tuesday night they flipped control of the state House, though Republicans held onto the state Senate with a two-seat margin. It’s possible some Republican senators will join Democrats to approve legislation, said Chris Cooper, a professor of political science and public affairs at Western Carolina University in Cullowhee, North Carolina. But he wouldn’t count on it. “I think the greater possibility really is that we see very little, that we just see stalemate coming out of Raleigh and if you’re a Republican, maybe that’s not so bad,” Cooper told NC Newsline on Wednesday. The GOP has already ticked off many of the items on its legislative wish list since gaining power in 2011, he said. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has seen a dozen of his vetoes overridden by the GOP-controlled legislature. “If less happens in Raleigh and you’re a conservative Republican, I’m not sure you’re that upset about that,” Cooper said. “It’s the Democrats who still wouldn’t be able to act.” In Texas, where Democrats hadn’t won a statewide office since 1994, they swept all statewide offices and flipped control of the state House. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to declare a “high-cost emergency” in Texas and to issue executive orders to suspend the state gas and diesel taxes and to freeze electricity rates. But Senate Republicans, who held the upper chamber Tuesday, have promised to oppose her. “Texas stands as long as the Texas Senate Republican caucus holds the line,” Republican state Sen. Charles Schwertner posted on X Tuesday night. “We will.” Focusing on pocketbooks In Arizona, Democratic lawmakers say they’re focused squarely on affordability. “In Arizona, lots of people have lost their SNAP (food stamp) benefits, and lots of people are having a really hard time affording their rent and their mortgages,” said Gutierrez. She said her caucus will aim to ban grocery stores from using dynamic pricing to gouge consumers; control rent hikes; and try to make homes more affordable by placing restrictions on corporate property purchases, which can drive up prices. Arizona Democrats also want to constrain a state program that allows K-12 students to receive public funding to pay for private school tuition. In Missouri, Republicans are questioning their legislative agenda after losing 16 House seats in their worst performance since the Watergate scandal. The GOP maintained its majority but lost its supermajority status. “We’re in a total reassessment,” Rep. Darin Chappell, who was selected as the House majority leader, told The Missouri Independent. Other Republican lawmakers said they needed to focus more on voters’ affordability priorities and less on legislative pet projects. “People have been speaking loud and clear that they want us to focus on issues that affect their pocketbooks,” said state Rep. Israel Baeza, a Republican. Major Republican losses in Utah deprived the GOP of a legislative supermajority for the first time since 1993. While Republicans maintain total control of state government, this week’s “blue tsunami” could cause leadership shakeups and reshape policy priorities, the Utah News Dispatch reported. Democratic state lawmakers must act quickly to capitalize on their momentum, said Gaby Goldstein, the founder and president of State Futures, a nonprofit that coordinates hundreds of Democratic lawmakers across the states. She said states have the ability to immediately alleviate affordability pressures by bringing down the costs of prescription drugs, erasing medical debt and addressing labor issues such as minimum wages. “These are policies that have a big, immediate impact on people’s lives, and can tell that broader story about why people’s lives are different when Democrats are in power,” she said. After winning control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats are poised to launch investigations and increase oversight of the Trump administration. But Goldstein said state Democrats must deliver on the affordability promises they made to get into power. “It needs to result in people’s lives feeling appreciably better if Democrats want to hold on to power in ‘28,” she said. “At the federal level, the story has to roll up from what Democrats have done at the state level because oversight hearings are going to feel good, but they’re not putting any money in your pocket.” Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.title: Young home shoppers still priced out without help, according to survey
articles.description: The age of the typical first-time homebuyer last year remained stuck at a historic high of 40 years old as younger people continue to get the worst of brutally high prices and interest rates in much of the country. That’s according to new data from the National Association of Realtors, and it’s the second year […]
articles.content: A workman paints a door at a house under contract in Nanuet, N.Y. New York was ranked last and Indiana first among states for affordability and home building by a realtors.com report this year. (Photo by Tim Henderson/Stateline)The age of the typical first-time homebuyer last year remained stuck at a historic high of 40 years old as younger people continue to get the worst of brutally high prices and interest rates in much of the country. That’s according to new data from the National Association of Realtors, and it’s the second year in a row that the median age of first-time buyers was 40, after being as low as 28 years old in 1991. An increasing number of first-time homebuyers are using all cash rather than taking a mortgage, and those are even older, typically 54, said Jessica Lautz, the association’s deputy chief economist and vice president of research. Cash purchases are usually because of inheritances or other family help. “That’s actually 1 in 10 first-time buyers, so we’re really seeing that generational transfer of wealth,” Lautz said of cash offers. Repeat homebuyers also remained at a median 62 years old, also an all-time high, according to the report. The Bay Area near San Francisco is an area where prices are still escalating because of the AI boom, Lautz said, though some Rust Belt areas and states building a lot of housing are seeing more reasonable prices. A realtor.com report in June ranked Indiana, Iowa, South Carolina, Texas, North Carolina and Nebraska highest for affordability and homebuilding rates, based on prices compared to income and new building permits. At the bottom: New York, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Hawaii and California. Including cash sales is one reason the National Association of Realtors’ survey of homebuyers found a higher median age than other surveys, such as the New York Federal Reserve Bank’s review of mortgage applications, Lautz said. The Federal Reserve pegs the median age at 33 for first-time buyers for the first six months of 2026, said Yanling Mayer, a research economist for the Texas Real Estate Research Center at Texas A&M University. That’s about the same as in 2019, while the Realtors’ association survey — which includes cash purchases — recorded a jump from 33 years old in 2019, to 40 for the past two years. “We’re certainly not brushing aside the challenges facing first-time homebuyers,” Mayer said. “Are they finding other means to achieve home ownership? Help from family, help from friends?” There were several surveys last year that generally showed first-time buyers at between 35 and 40 years old and getting older, said Eric Finnigan, vice president of demographics research for John Burns Research and Consulting. “The answer is probably somewhere in the middle,” Finnigan said.
