How Abdul El-Sayed actually did with Jewish voters
articles.content: Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson rode a “blue wave” to win Michigan’s US Senate and governor’s races, respectively, outperforming recent party performance in an election that was a rebuke of President Donald Trump. Benson, a Democrat, will succeed outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer after beating Republican John James by more than 10 percentage points, according to unofficial results. El-Sayed, a progressive who campaigned on universal healthcare and taxing the rich, defeated Republican Mike Rogers by about seven points, defending the seat to help Democrats retake control of the US Senate. Here’s a look at how they secured victory: El-Sayed and Benson both benefited from relatively high turnout across the state, particularly among Democratic voters. According to unofficial results, more than 4.8 million voters cast ballots in Michigan. That appears to be a midterm record, topping the 4.5 million Michiganders who voted in 2022 but shy of the 5.7 million who cast ballots in the 2024 presidential election that Trump won. Benson won 18 counties, while El-Sayed won 14, including several of the most populous counties that helped make up for losses in more rural areas. But even in the counties they lost, Benson and El-Sayed exceeded expectations. All 83 Michigan counties shifted toward Democrats compared with the 2024 election, according to an analysis by the Associated Press. That included a 14-percentage point shift in Wayne County, the state’s largest, but also double-digit shifts in more rural areas like Dickinson, Branch and St. Joseph counties. In Wexford County, where Rogers won by a smaller margin than two years ago, retired Manton voter Jerrilyn Mathews, a former Republican, said she voted for El-Sayed, other Democrats and “anything against Trump.” As of 7 a.m., about 93% of all Wayne County ballots had been counted with El-Sayed and Benson each getting more than 70% of the vote in their respective races, according to unofficial results. Both outperformed 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, who topped Trump with 63% of the Wayne County vote in 2024. In Detroit, the state’s largest city, Benson won about 93% of the vote and El-Sayed won about 92%, according to unofficial results. Both topped the 90% Harris won in Detroit two years ago. Rogers spent considerable time in Detroit and touted inroads with Democrats, including outgoing state Rep. Karen Whitsett. But he received only 5% of the city vote in Tuesday’s election, down from the 7% he won there in his 2024 loss to US Sen. Elissa Slotkin. “I voted to go against Trump. When it all comes down to it, we are trying to vote against Trump,” said Henry McCoi of Detroit, who cast his ballot at Mayberry Elementary School. Rogers also heavily courted Jewish voters turned off by El-Sayed’s opposition to US support for Israel and comments in the wake of a March attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township. Unofficial results show Rogers did improve his vote share in some Oakland County communities with heavy Jewish populations, but he did not gain enough ground to make up for Democratic shifts in other parts of the county and state. In West Bloomfield Township, for instance, Rogers won 46% of the vote, up from 42% in 2024. El-Sayed won the township by 2,240 votes, down from the 5,538-vote margin Slotkin won it by two years ago. All told, El-Sayed won Oakland County with 56% of the vote, topping Harris’ 54% in 2024. In Huntington Woods, which El-Sayed carried, 55-year-old Lauren Slutsky described herself as a lifelong Jewish Democrat but said she voted for Rogers because El-Sayed “hasn’t proven that he will stand against antisemitism and hate.” At the same polling place, Steve Gold stood wearing a “Jews for Abdul” shirt and praised El-Sayed’s push for Medicare for All, calling it “shameful that the United States has not provided healthcare to everybody after 250 years.” Meanwhile, some metro Detroit communities with larger Muslim populations that had broken for Trump two years ago shifted back to Democrats on Tuesday. Trump won Dearborn by six percentage points in 2024, but El-Sayed won the city by 65 points on Tuesday, and Benson won it by 60 points, according to unofficial results. Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud said the city’s 45,464-voter turnout was the highest ever. College towns also helped secure victories for El-Sayed and Benson. With nearly all ballots counted in Washtenaw County, El-Sayed won there with 74% of the vote. Benson received about 75%. Both outperformed Harris, who had won 71% of Washtenaw County votes in 2024. El-Sayed and Benson also outperformed Harris in Ingham, Kalamazoo, Isabella and Kent counties, all home to universities and large groups of young voters. Jack Morean, a 19-year-old Michigan State University student from Grand Rapids, voted in his first general election Tuesday morning at an on-campus precinct in East Lansing. Morean said he voted for Democrats up and down his ballot. “We’re in a time where divisiveness is very apparent,” he said. “Our current government is honestly abhorrent. I’m here to vote for change.” Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan. articles.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
articles.description: Certain configurations of Alpine are affected. Other distros may be as well.
articles.content: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations. One connection, works every time, needs no retries There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.Read full article Comments

articles.content: Social media cntent creator duo Josh & Jase (Joshua Cauldwell-Clarke and Jason “Jase” Riley) are back in Michigan, encouraging their fanbase to give back by donating blood. The two partnered with the Big Ten Conference and global healthcare organization Abbott for the third annual “We Give Blood” drive, a national competition to increase turnout to blood drives. Social media content creator duo Josh & Jase (Joshua Cauldwell-Clarke and Jason “Jase” Riley) are back in Michigan, encouraging their fanbase to give back by donating blood. Photo by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse The competition involves all Big Ten schools, and a $1 million grant for student or community health goes to the winner. At the Kellogg Hotel and Conference Center on Michigan State University’s campus, the two posed for photos with blood donors. According to Cauldwell-Clarke, the organizers of the competition reached out to the pair after they put a call out on social media. “We want to use our platform for good,” he said. “There’s a shortage at the moment of young people donating blood … that’s our mission, getting people [to donate].” “There is no point in having lots of followers or a big platform if you’re not using it,” counterpart Riley said. The duo’s presence pulled in a lot of interest from potential donors. “We have a completely full schedule,” Caitlin Gallagher said. “We’ve had 115 appointments and a lot more people walk in too.” Gallagher works with Versiti, the health organization overseeing the drive. Social media content creator duo Josh & Jase (Joshua Cauldwell-Clarke and Jason “Jase” Riley) are back in Michigan, encouraging their fanbase to give back by donating blood. Photo by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Keegan Wynn attends Michigan State University and is a student ambassador with Abbott. He has watched Josh & Jase a few times on social media but did not expect them to be on MSU’s campus. “So when this opportunity came up, and I saw they’d be partnering with ‘We Give Blood,’ it was kind of unexpected.” Wynn planned on getting a picture with the pair later on in the afternoon. This is the duo’s second trip to Michigan, announced Oct. 25 via social media, and includes attending the MSU versus University of Michigan football game on Nov. 7. “This could be one of the best college experiences we’re ever gonna have,” Cauldwell-Clarke said. As for the rest of their time in East Lansing, they plan on exploring more of Michigan’s capital and MSU’s campus.

articles.title: Hertel chosen as state Senate Majority Floor Leader
articles.content: Democratic state Sen. Kevin Hertel of St. Clair Shores was elected Thursday to serve as Majority Floor Leader for Michigan’s 104th Legislature starting Jan. 1. “I am deeply honored to have earned the confidence of my Democratic colleagues to serve as Floor Leader,” Hertel said in a press release from his office. “Our job as legislators is not simply to talk about the policies we want to see passed — it’s to do the hard work of getting them across the finish line. This means working across the aisle and building consensus to tackle the challenges facing our state.” State Sen. Darrin Camilleri, D-Trenton, was elected the new Majority Leader, replacing Sen. Winnie Brinks, D-Grand Rapids, who was elected Lieutenant Governor on Tuesday. Camilleri and Hertel were chosen during a closed caucus meeting. “In this new leadership role, I look forward to working hand-in-hand with Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri as we set an ambitious agenda and turn our policy priorities into real results: lowered costs, expanded opportunity, and a stronger Michigan where working families can get ahead,” Hertel added. Camilleri said, “Voters sent a clear message on Tuesday. They are fed up with the kind of politics that has repeatedly ignored the needs of working-class families. They want leaders who are ready to take the gloves off and actually fight to lower costs and deliver on their promises.” “We want to make sure with this diverse caucus that everybody, everybody’s ideas are on the table, that every voice is being heard, and that we are being extremely productive,” Hertel told reporters, according to Michigan Advance. “That’s the role of the floor leader to make sure everything’s moving in a smooth fashion. That the caucus is getting the information that they need.” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr., who is Kevin Hertel’s brother, congratulated both men. “Senators Camilleri and Hertel are proven fighters who will work to drive down costs and stand up for working families,” Curtis Hertel said. “With historic majorities in both chambers, Michigan Democrats are working to immediately deliver for the people of Michigan.” The Hertel brothers are the sons of Curtis Hertel Sr., who was House Majority Leader. Former state senator, Michigan State Fair Director and Macomb County Commissioner John Hertel of Lenox Township is their uncle. Kevin Hertel won his second 4-year term Tuesday in a fairly close race over GOP challenger John Goldwater by 51.4% to 48.15% for the 12th District, which covers eastern Macomb County and St. Clair counties, and the Grosse Pointes. Hertel served in the Michigan House of Representatives from 2016-2022. He is a member of several committees, including Appropriations. Camilleri was re-elected Tuesday to represent the 4th District, which covers several communities in the southern suburban, downriver area of Wayne County and western Wayne County. Camilleri and Hertel have followed similar paths as lawmakers. Camilleri also served three terms as a state representative before being elected a senator four years ago. He will also be the first majority leader from Wayne County in over 40 years.

articles.title: FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to a New Treatment for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
articles.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval to Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherap
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval to Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. HNSCC is an aggressive, life-threatening disease for which there is a high unmet need for effective therapies. Rybrevant Faspro is not indicated as a treatment for patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma that is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Approval was based on trial results showing that more than double the percentage of patients responded to the drug compared to currently approved therapies. This is the first approval in 10 years of a drug for patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC who had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. “Today’s approval represents a meaningful step forward for patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a disease where treatment options have historically been limited and outcomes remain poor,” said Angelo De Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “This therapy offers patients and their physicians a new option with the potential to make a real difference in people’s lives.” The Accelerated Approval Program allows for earlier approval of drugs that treat serious conditions and fill an unmet medical need based on surrogate or intermediate endpoints. In this case, accelerated approval of Rybrevant Faspro was granted based on overall response rate and duration of response. Since it is not yet confirmed whether this will translate into a clinically meaningful benefit in long-term outcomes, the FDA has required confirmatory studies to verify and describe clinical benefit. In an open-label, multicenter clinical trial involving 102 patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, Rybrevant Faspro had an overall response rate of 42%, meaning these patients saw their tumor either decrease in size or disappear. Of those patients who had a response, 56% had a response lasting six months or longer. Currently approved therapies are associated with an overall response rate of around 20% or less and poor outcomes. The prescribing information for use as a single agent includes warnings and precautions for hypersensitivity and administration-related reactions, interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, dermatologic adverse reactions, ocular toxicity, and harm to an unborn baby. The FDA granted Rybrevant Faspro Breakthrough Therapy designation for this indication. The approval was granted to Janssen Biotech, Inc. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

articles.content: Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use. Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan. Three ways the 2026 midterm election could impact Michigan’s environment
articles.description: Winning candidates will be able to influence environmental policies and voters had their say on energy regulation, data centers and more.
articles.content: (Kate Furby / Michigan Public)Somehow I spent Election Day reporting on snails. I don’t really understand how it happened either. While my colleagues were driving around Michigan covering events and reporting in from polling places and parties, speaking with Michiganders about this historic and dramatic Senate race, I was here in the office calling up scientists and gleefully shouting out snail facts.Let’s talk about how some of the election results may impact environmental issues moving forward.Data centersData centers were certainly on the ballot this election. They were a prominent talking point in the tight race for the House in Michigan’s 7th District, which William Lawrence won.Democrat Jocelyn Benson was elected governor of Michigan. Her campaign stated support for a temporary moratorium on data centers. Her website calls for "requiring developers to prove prior to construction that the data center will not abuse natural resources - from water to land.” This statement is vague, so it’s hard to say at this point what that would mean in practice.Garlin Gilchrist won the election for Michigan Secretary of State. In a statement to Planet Detroit, he listed flooding, poor air quality and extreme heat as environmental priorities for the state. He also emphasized data center companies’ responsibility for water use and water quality impacts.Science and the environmentMichigan Democratic Attorney General candidate Eli Savit speaks to supporters on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026 at Hudson's Detroit. Savit defeated Republican Doug Lloyd in the AG race.(Zena Issa / Michigan Public )Eli Savit won the Michigan Attorney General race. He told Michigan Public’s Caoilinn Goss that environmental protections were something he cared about protecting as part of our democracy. Attorney generals have a key role in defending science and the environment. Earlier this year, Attorney General Dana Nessel joined other states in signing a letter opposing legislation that would have made government science funding processes more partisan.A millage (a.k.a. a tax) was approved to help support the Detroit Zoo and several Detroit museums, including the Belle Isle Dossin Great Lakes Museum.Energy In Ann Arbor, Proposal E, which would have started the process of changing the city’s electric infrastructure to establish a municipal utility, narrowly failed to pass.Eli Savit’s win may also be important for Michigan’s energy future. Current Attorney General Nessel filed multiple requests challenging the J.H. Campbell power plant, for example.State-level challenges of the Trump administration environmental and energy regulation will continue to be incredibly important to watch. And how each candidate rises to their campaign promises, especially how those promises relate to our clean air and water, is something I’m personally interested in following as well.Let's end on snailsNew Zealand mudsnail shells found in Bear Creek macroinvertebrate samples. (Coldwater River Watershed Council)One of the scientists I spoke with on Tuesday said she was super happy to talk about anything but the election. So in case you’re also exhausted from this election news cycle, I’ll just end with some mind-blowing facts about the invasive New Zealand mudsnails:So far, all snails found in Michigan have been female.They can reproduce asexually, so just one female snail arrival in a new location could herald a new era of snail dominance.This snail’s shell has a little trapdoor that lets it duck inside and shut the door. Some of them have been found to survive inside a fish digestive tract using this! This means that they are incredible survivors and a terrible meal for fish.Have more news for me? Have a hot tip? Send your ballot-based environmental concerns to furby@umich.edu.‘Til next week,Kate Furby, Senior Environment Reporter_______________________________Today’s newsletter was written by Kate Furby, produced by Michelle Keller, and edited by Rebecca Williams.

articles.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.description: Google is technically offering schools more choice but not the choices anyone wants.
articles.content: Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools. Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn't want to use AI. Google didn't see the backlash coming, but now that it's here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what's changing. The gist of the new policy, according to Google's blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. When Google revealed its new policy, the company's VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times, which interpreted the situation as Google will "turn off search" if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it's probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google's educational AI system will operate. Google's approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.Read full article Comments

articles.content: ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing. A grand jury indicted Cheryl Gates on charges of attempted first-degree murder and food contamination in October. About a week prior, the accusations that ChatGPT was a co-conspirator in the attempted murder came in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that was made public this week. In it, James Gates alleged that OpenAI and Sam Altman failed to employ technical safeguards to shut down Cheryl’s chats even after her queries became “obviously suspicious” and sought advice on how to execute and conceal a homicide. At first, Cheryl told ChatGPT that she was researching poisoning out of fear that her husband might possibly try to kill her—framing her queries as “self-protection.” Coming to the rescue, ChatGPT did not terminate the conversation. Instead, it helped her “with specific instructions for the preparation, dosage, and administration of Oleander, including whether anti-nausea medicine would accelerate or inhibit death, whether it would show on an autopsy report, and whether it could be injected into a vein or muscle instead of being ingested in tea and have the same lethal effect,” the lawsuit said.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Ken Ziffren Offers Optimistic View On Industry, Even When It Comes To AI & Federal Tax Credit Legislation
articles.description: “The state of the theater industry is perhaps on the up,” Ken Ziffren told a ballroom of entertainment lawyers Thursday after a recent strong box office. In his annual look at the industry, the Hollywood legal mandarin put AI, tax credits, the creator economy, M&A, YouTube, the NFL and more in the spotlight along with […]
articles.content: “The state of the theater industry is perhaps on the up,” Ken Ziffren told a ballroom of entertainment lawyers Thursday after a recent strong box office. In his annual look at the industry, the Hollywood legal mandarin put AI, tax credits, the creator economy, M&A, YouTube, the NFL and more in the spotlight along with the current state of moviegoing. As usual, Ziffren’s hourlong speech was a data wonk’s dream, but it also was noticeably more upbeat than in past years. It also doesn’t hurt that when it comes to box office registers, Ziffren is right. Watch on Deadline The box office is headed to its best year both stateside and global since pre-Covid 2019, with a respective projected $10 billion and near $36 billion. Despite the recent merger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery, Ziffren seemed hopeful that the future of moviegoing wasn’t bound to dim. “Hoping that it’s a successful merger and that it’s not one as others,” said Ziffren. RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office Putting Skydance’s $111 billion Para and WBD merger in context with the massive SpaceX IPO and looming stock market moves by Anthropic and OpenAI, the Ziffren Brittenham LLP co-founder summarized M&A activity as a mixed economic bag. The YouTube and ESPN deal, with the NFL Network purchase, got some special attention as did the recent revival of the big-bucks Sunday Ticket class action. “Where that’s going to go is anyone guess,” Ziffren said of the case, pondering if the NFL would move to take the matter to the Supreme Court. The attorney also noted that the Sunday Ticket plaintiffs can file a new case now that the bundle is off DirecTV and on YouTube. RELATED: Bob Iger’s New Magic Kingdom: Fans & Media Wonder If He Can Bring That Disney Sparkle To The Lakers The NBA — or, more specifically, the L.A. Lakers — received some legal attention from Ziffren with the messy situation of the Buss family civil war that has broken out over their stake in the team with Bob Iger and Josh Kushner’s $12.5 billion purchase in August. A court hearing is set for the Bass sibling squabble on November 15, 2026 in downtown LA. Turning to a past fave topic of tax credits, Ziffren offered an overview of the proposed The Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, currently before committees in the Senate and House of Representatives. “This legislation is needed by our industry,” Ziffren exclaimed, noting competition and incentives for production globally from more than 65 countries and other jurisdictions. To hit the bottom line, Ziffren opined that the passage of the bipartisan MPTER Act would lead to a surge in production jobs stateside and “$10 billion” for the industry in terms of production. RELATED: Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor Supported by strange bedfellows from Donald Trump to Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) even before this week’s midterms, the legislation would let productions eligible for the credit include film and TV productions where the total cost exceeds $1 million and where 75% of the production is in the U.S. There also are provisions for post-production and visual effects. Excluded are news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising and corporate videos. Ziffren hoped the “bipartisan period” of the current lame duck Congress would see the federal tax credit pass before the end of the year. Still, with a deeper look at the big screen, Ziffren emphasized that for the most part, outside of horror films, whenever studios make films that cost under $70M, they tend to lose money. To him, this underscores the vitality of a tentpole investment mind-set at the motion picture studios. RELATED: Top 50 Classic Horror Movies: A Photo Gallery “Wide releases are essential to keep that [moviegoing] attendance stable and growing,” Ziffren said. This despite the fall of wide release movies from a level of roughly 100 pre-Covid to 75 in 2024. That number has increased to 94 this year. While studios pivoted to a day-and-date release model during Covid, when theaters were closed, Ziffren made a point Thursday to underscore how profitable the downstream business is for studios. “Studios can get a lot of money in licensing,” he said, noting that a pay one window can reap as much as $250 million. After PVOD, studios are licensing to their sister companies in the ad-supported business in what is another lucrative window. “It’s a profitable business once you get in the TV world,” he explained, specifying how the pay TV (or streaming) business has become one with and without commercials. “The only costs in distribution are remittance taxes and residuals, and now and then profit participations,” Ziffren added. RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office To that, with a mild swipe at algorhythms, Ziffren noted that for all the worries about the effect artificial intelligence will have on the entertainment industry, execs should pay attention to the bottom line. Advocating for studios and streamers to lean into quality over quantity in their battle for eyeballs with YouTube, TikTok, and META’s Instagram, the lawyer noted that AI already has shown it can cut costs. AI will “lower the costs of post and pre-production, and ultimately production itself,” he noted, as he also said how that will play put in terms of investment is “anyone’s guess.” As far as the masses’ reception to AI in entertainment, Ziffren acknowledged that “audiences demand will continue to value premium crafted storytelling.” That’s a consensus that many film tracking firms would agree with Ziffren on: Gen-Z audiences have been turned off by the whole notion of AI. It’s a reason why Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has been so successful grossing $1.8B, Universal and the filmmaker’s top grossing movie ever. Younger audiences have savored the physical craftsmanship on screen. Harking back to the state of Tinseltown labor, which was the heart of Ziffen’s 2025 speech, the lawyer stated, “AI was not a major issue as it was in 2023.” Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy. articles.title: DTE, Consumers sue to block ‘money out of politics’ proposal approved by voters
articles.description: Michigan’s biggest utility companies are suing to block implementation of Proposal 2, arguing voter-approved restrictions on political giving violate free speech rights.
articles.content: Michigan utilities sue over Proposal 2, which passed Tuesday with more than 80% of the vote Law bans utilities and some state contractors from donating to political campaigns, among other things Lawsuit alleges that violates free speech and other constitutional rights LANSING — Two days after Michigan voters overwhelmingly approved Proposal 2, DTE Energy and Consumers Energy on Thursday sued to stop implementation of new restrictions on their political giving. The state’s largest utilities argue that the new law — approved by more than 80% of voters in Tuesday’s election — will violate their free speech rights and other provisions of the US Constitution. Proposal 2 aims to prohibit direct or indirect contributions to Michigan politicians by the utilities or companies with more than $250,000 in state government contracts, along with immediate family members and other people with close connections. But in a complaint filed with the US District Court for the Western District of Michigan, the utilities argued the proposal violates free speech and association rights guaranteed by the First Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment’s due process clause. Absent an injunction, the companies “will be forced to choose between surrendering their rights to political association and risking substantial penalties for exercising them,” attorneys wrote. Policymakers and voters benefit from hearing Consumers’ perspective on debates over reliability, affordability and clean energy “even if they may sometimes disagree with it,” they added. Related: Michigan elections: Voters approve Proposal 2 Money Out of Politics question Michigan midterm voters cite costs, government spending, culture wars and Trump Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems The suit seeks a court order barring enforcement by the state. It names Michigan Bureau of Elections Director Jonathan Brater, Attorney General Dana Nessel and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (now the governor-elect) as defendants. The lawsuit is “no surprise,” said Maura Cowley, manager of the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, which argues the law will “end pay-to-play politics” in Lansing. “The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before,” Cowley said in a statement. The group is “confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this and any legal challenge,” she added. Donate It’s already the second lawsuit over Proposal 2. The Mackinac Center for Public Policy announced a legal challenge Tuesday night after it became clear voters had approved the measure. While opposition groups had argued the proposal would violate free speech rights, the utility lawsuit argues the new law also violates the Fourteenth Amendment because it is too vague in its reasons as to why utilities shouldn’t be able to continue donating to candidates — as well as who the proposal applies to working at or with these companies. The complaint also contends the law violates the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause by “impermissibly” targeting utilities “and a broad swath of people associated with utilities.” The US Supreme Court has generally held that political spending by corporations is protected speech, most notably in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, but courts have looked more favorably on narrowly tailored proposals aimed at limiting corruption. The law “unfairly targets a Michigan business,” along with its employees and their families, Consumers Energy spokesperson Katie Carey said in a statement. “Michiganders should not lose their First Amendment rights because of where they work.” Corporations are already barred from directly giving to candidates in Michigan. The proposal would extend that ban to an affected company’s president, CEO, treasurer, similar officials, board members, people with “substantial” ownership — and their family members. One of the plaintiffs in the suit is the 86-year-old mother of DTE’s treasurer, who would be barred from donating to political candidates “even though she has no role at any utility,” according to the suit. The proposal would restrict political contributions to: The governor, attorney general, state senator, representative or candidate for such office A state or local party committee A committee, other than an independent expenditure committee or ballot question committee, that makes contributions to a candidate A member of the Michigan Public Service Commission Company officials and immediate family members could also not donate to entities that are affiliated with elected officials or candidates and pay for their travel, meals, conference fees or other expenses. Consumers and DTE have spent on political races through employee-funded PACs and “dark money” nonprofits that don’t have to disclose donors. The proposal would require disclosure by groups that reference candidates or ballot issues in so-called issue ads. The proposal would not prohibit contributions to independent expenditure super PACs allowed under Citizens United, but it includes language that had anticipated potential legal challenges: “If any portion is found void, invalid or unenforceable, the remaining portions remain in effect.”

articles.title: MPSC sets December deadline for decision on Consumers Energy dam sales
articles.description: Consumers Energy, one of the state’s largest energy utilities, has once again asked Michigan energy regulators to delay their decision on whether to approve a sale of 13 hydroelectric dams located throughout the state. While the Michigan Public Service Commission’s three members unanimously approved Consumers’ request to delay decision-making during their Thursday meeting, Chair Dan […]
articles.content: Foote Dam in Iosco County, one of 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Photo from Consumers Energy)Consumers Energy, one of the state’s largest energy utilities, has once again asked Michigan energy regulators to delay their decision on whether to approve a sale of 13 hydroelectric dams located throughout the state. While the Michigan Public Service Commission’s three members unanimously approved Consumers’ request to delay decision-making during their Thursday meeting, Chair Dan Scripps stressed that this would be the final extension, unless a majority of the parties in the case agree to another. “Any settlement agreement must be filed by 5 p.m. on Dec. 9, 2026, and any further extension of the waiver of the statutory deadline would require a stipulation from a majority of the parties to the proceeding that must be filed on that same date,” Scripps said. If the parties do not reach a settlement, the commission will issue a final order at its Dec. 17 meeting, Scripps said. Consumers Energy filed its first request to delay the commission’s decision on Sept. 8, stating it felt they could come to a constructive solution regarding some of the concerns raised by the parties opposing the sale. However, the company’s call for a compromise was met with skepticism by multiple environmental and conservation organizations opposing the sale. Daniel Abrams, a senior associate attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center, wrote in opposition to the request, stating “This is not a case in which the parties are fully and deeply engaged in ongoing negotiations that are close to resolution.” That skepticism had not faded when the company filed its latest request on Tuesday. While Consumers Energy Attorney Bret Totoraitis said the company believes “there continues to be opportunity for a constructive settlement solution in this case that addresses the concerns raised during the course of the proceeding and wishes to continue to engage in negotiations to achieve such a solution,” Abrams disputed that assessment. Michigan AG urges state regulators to reject Consumers Energy dam sale “Simply put, this case is not going to settle,” Abrams wrote in his response on behalf of Michigan Trout Unlimited, the Michigan Steelhead and Salmon Fishermen’s Association, Great Lakes Council of Fly Fishers International, Anglers of the Au Sable and the Michigan Hydro Relicensing Coalition. Consumers Energy announced it had found a buyer for the collection of dams in 2025. Under the conditions of the sale, Confluence Hydro – a subsidiary of Hull Street Energy, a Maryland-based private equity company – will purchase the dams for $1 each and enter a contract with Consumers Energy to provide them with power from the dams for 30 years. However, several parties, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Attorney General Dan Nessel, have raised safety concerns around selling the dams, which were built between 1906 and 1935, to an out-of-state private equity company. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “These dams are powerful, and they can be dangerous when they’re not maintained,” Nessel told Michigan Advance in an Oct. 21 interview. “So any sale that takes 13 dams in Michigan out of the hands of a well-funded and highly regulated public utility, and then gives it to the interests of out-of-state private equity, we think, should be looked at very carefully and candidly, very skeptically.” In a letter to the public service commission, Whitmer argued that the deal around the sale “lacks firm, enforceable protections to ensure the dams will be properly maintained and safely retired when they are no longer economical to operate.” “It does not require Hull Street Energy, the parent company, to cover all future repair, accident, environmental, and decommissioning costs, nor does it require adequately funded reserves to cover those expenses,” Whitmer wrote. If it is unable to move forward with the sale, Consumers Energy has said the dams will be decommissioned, sparking concerns among the communities who use the waterways created by these dams. However, Nessel told Michigan Advance that Consumers cannot make that decision on its own. “It would require entirely separate and lengthy cases before the MPSC, and the local communities get to have a say in that,” Nessel said. “But that wouldn’t be the case if they’re sold off to private equity.” In an email following Thursday’s commission meeting, Consumers Energy Media Relations Manager Brian Wheeler told the Advance the company appreciates the commissioners’ decision to establish a timetable to reach a settlement. “We understand the desire for communities and our coworkers to resolve this sale,” Chris Fultz, Consumers Energy’s senior vice president of electric supply said in a statement. “Today’s MPSC ruling keeps us on that path toward an agreement that will be a win for our customers, Michigan and the communities we care about.”

articles.description: Voters strongly supported funding local parks, museums, libraries and public safety.
articles.content: Michigan voters generally supported efforts to fund public safety, libraries, roads and parks. Eight communities rejected efforts to fund EMS, which could also impact fire and police services Retail cannabis is expanding in six communities Michigan voters overwhelmingly supported keeping their local emergency services funded this November general election. There were about 124 public safety millage questions on the ballot for various communities in the state, according to Gongwer News Service. Of that, only 14 failed to win support for fire departments, law enforcement or emergency medical services. Use the tool below to search results. Some 40 public safety millage proposals called for increasing local taxes for EMS as some communities struggle to keep ambulance services funded. Eight communities — Onekama Township, Cooper Township, Stronach Township, Clarkston, Secord Township, Gibraltar and Norvell Township — struck down those proposals. The decisions could also jeopardize fire and police funding in communities that combine those operations under one roof. Related: Majority of Michigan school bonds pass in Nov. election. Look up your district EMS providers battle money, staffing woes in rural Michigan’s ambulance ‘deserts’ Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect An assortment of “I Voted” stickers. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) Kent County rejected a 20-year jail millage, and Houghton County similarly passed on a $28 million public safety bond to build new jail facilities. Five cities passed proposals to create citizen-led healthcare advisory committees to draft policy recommendations. Lansing, East Lansing, Kalamazoo, Portage, and Benton Harbor approved the measures launched by the nonprofit City Action Michigan, an organization linked to unseating vulnerable Republicans in Congress. Other proposals to expand or maintain health-related services received mixed results. Senior services stand to receive renewed funding in all communities where it was on the ballot. A millage renewal to fund a rural health center on Lake Michigan’s Beaver Island secured funding, while an Ogemaw County proposal to fund trauma therapy for families who have experienced abuse failed to pass.Donate Corunna in Shiawassee County rejected efforts to adopt gender-neutral terminology within its charter. Growing cannabis support Marijuana businesses will be able to expand after voters decided to repeal prohibitions and authorize new establishments in six communities. Bad Axe, Menominee and Big Prairie Township passed measures to drop retail cannabis bans as Boyne Falls and Mottville Township voted down prohibitions on the industry. Near the Indiana-Michigan border, Niles Township failed to lift its cannabis ban, while the neighboring city of Niles capped its marijuana retailers at five and microbusinesses at four. Parks, libraries, roads and museums Library funding passed in most of the 20 communities where it was on the ballot, save for Geneva Township, Redding Township and Oscoda County. Parks and recreation millages similarly got approved in 19 communities, while efforts in Commerce Township, Byron Township, Durand, Miles Township, Owosso and Muskegon were voted down. Of the state’s 76 road millage and public works bond proposals, 22 failed to pass. Museums and zoos also had a good day — Oakland and Wayne counties approved public funding for the Detroit Historical Society and Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History. Voters also passed millages for the Detroit Zoo, the John Ball Zoo and Grand Rapids Public Museum.

articles.title: Declaration of final vote results in Serbia paves way for student movement to form government
articles.description: Declaration of final vote results in Serbia paves way for student movement to form government AP News Serbia has banished the monsters from Belgrade – it was, and still is, a truly wonderful revolution | Barbi Marković The Guardian After the landslide victory of the Students' List, Serbia's judiciary springs into action DW.com Serbia’s Gen Z Students Toppled a Strongman. Now Comes the Hard Part. WSJ Belgrade Diary: E
articles.content: BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia’s election authorities on Thursday declared the final results of the Oct. 25 vote, paving the way for the formation of a new Parliament and government that will be dominated by the student movement that defeated former strongman Aleksandar Vucic ‘s government. The Students’ List group will have 140 lawmakers in the 250-member assembly while Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party will have 103 lawmakers, the Republic Election Commission said. The rest of the parliamentary seats will belong to the parties of ethnic minorities in Serbia. The students led two years of street protests before they toppled Vucic in the election. Protests erupted in response to a train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the country’s north in November 2024, and which many in Serbia blamed on corruption in state infrastructure projects. The Students’ List election candidates included mostly professors, teachers and various other experts in their fields but with hardly any political experience, who will now take up parliamentary seats. The group promised to restore the rule of law and terminate corruption that they said flourished under Vucic. Serbian election rules now envisage that the election commission must formally allocate the parliamentary mandates to the candidates before an inaugural session of Parliament is then held within 30 days. Though the election winners have yet to take office, the change in the balance of power has led to a series of detentions relating to cases of suspected election fraud, attacks on student protesters and corruption. Vucic has accused his opponents of a “revolutionary terror” though his right-wing party still controls the outgoing government and police. The SNS party has ruled the country almost unchallenged for 14 years, controlling all layers of power and state institutions. The party has faced accusations of corruption and cronyism and of organized crime links, which it has denied. Those detained so far include senior police officials, a bank owner and various other officials, such as the head of Serbia’s meteorological institute whom prosecutors suspect of money laundering. On Wednesday evening, nine policemen were detained for alleged torture and harassment of protesting students last August. The suspects included the commander of an elite anti-terrorist unit, Igor Zmiric. The student movement’s victory has resonated beyond Serbia’s borders at a time when many European countries face youth-led protests. Serbia is formally seekin g European Union entry but the process has stalled under Vucic, who has maintained close relations with Russia and China.

When BMW debuted the new 7 Series in 2022, it set a new standard for large luxury sedans, increasingly irrelevant though that class is. Rather than siloing off an electric alternative like Mercedes, with its EQS alongside the normal S-Class, BMW simply made the powertrain an option. Stick with a V8 if you want, or consider the rather good electric version instead—only subtle differences like the badging and lack of exhaust pipes give the game away. Since then, BMW has brought out a string of even newer electric vehicles for the 5 and 3 Series (plus their SUV counterparts). It has switched from battery packs made of prismatic cells to more energy-dense arrangements of cylindrical cells. The motors are still electrically excited synchronous ones, but now the drive units feature silicon carbide inverters and more compact packaging. This sixth-generation electric powertrain was designed for the clean-sheet Neue Klasse family, which also threw out the legacy cruft of dozens and dozens of discrete single-function electronic control units for a handful of powerful domain controllers. articles.title: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.description: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests AP News Were These Ancient Siberian Nomads the First Stoners? The New York Times Cannabis was used as an intoxicant as early as 2,800 years ago Phys.org Earliest evidence of cannabis use found in ancient Siberian tomb CNN Ancient humans were using cannabis far earlier in history than we thought Scientific American
articles.content: GENEVA (AP) — People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests. Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes. The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China. Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands. The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant’s role in ancient societies. “It’s extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context,” said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern. It’s not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said. The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians — ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine. The team, deployed “essentially out in the middle of nowhere,” lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe. Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear and animal-style motifs. But the team “struck gold” as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said. “It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that’s been dead for almost 3,000 years,” he said. Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and “they are not there by accident” but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said. Results were published Thursday in the journal Science. Not all independent experts were convinced. The hair analysis “is scientifically weak” and there’s not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email. “For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible,” Auwaerter said. “This matters because the hair data carry the abstract’s main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties).” Today, scholars don’t consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses — seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth — their presence alone doesn’t confirm drug use. Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn’t distinguish consumption from external exposure — in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange. But Elisa Guerra Doce of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study. In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that “cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite.”

articles.description: Unless the company can reach a settlement with critics, state regulators said they will rule on the controversial sale on Dec. 17.
articles.content: State utility regulators have set a December deadline to rule on the Consumers Energy dam sale Unless the utility can show negotiations with sale critics are bearing fruit, regulators will make a decision Dec. 17 Consumers calls the sale best for its ratepayers; critics contend it’s too risky and expensive Michigan regulators on Thursday gave Consumers Energy one last chance to negotiate with critics of its controversial plan to sell 13 Michigan dams to a private equity company. But unless those negotiations are fruitful, this is the last extension regulators will give before deciding whether to approve or reject the sale on Dec. 17. “Absent a firm showing that a critical mass of parties beyond Consumers remain interested in settlement, this will be the final extension,” said Dan Scripps, chair of the Michigan Public Service Commission. The three-person commission was originally poised to rule on the sale in September, but Consumers has twice sought last-minute extensions as it works to win over critics who see the sale as a bad deal for ratepayers and the public. RELATED: In Michigan, 100K live downstream of old, decrepit dams. ‘We’re at their mercy’ Federal policy shields safety details of many Michigan dams. Foes demand change Long-awaited dam safety reforms move closer to law after Michigan Senate vote After a month of talks with little progress, company officials say they still hope to reach a settlement. “We are providing for a little more time to reach a constructive agreement that will be a win for our customers, Michigan and the communities we care about,” said Chris Fultz, the utility’s senior vice president of electric supply. But sale opponents — including state environmental regulators, utility ratepayer advocates, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and outside environmental groups — argue the company is merely stalling for time. “It’s time for Consumers to stop the delay,” said Bob Stuber, executive director of the Michigan Hydro Relicensing Coalition. “They have had plenty of time.” For years, Consumers has been looking to exit a hydropower business that generates little power at an enormous cost. The 13 century-old dams on the Au Sable, Grand, Kalamazoo, Manistee and Muskegon rivers generate just 1% of the utility’s annual power output and need hundreds of millions of dollars in upgrades to keep operating.Donate Rather than making that investment or decommissioning the dams, Consumers wants to sell them for $1 apiece to Confluence Hydro, a newly created subsidiary of the Maryland private equity firm Hull Street Energy. Consumers would then commit its customers to buy back the power generated by the dams at twice the market rate, plus a $270 million cut to Consumers, which has vowed to funnel those profits into a dam safety fund. The deal would cost $3.4 billion over the life of the 30-year contract, or about $1,800 per person if divided equally among Consumers’ 1.9 million ratepayers Consumers contends that is hundreds of millions cheaper than keeping or demolishing the dams, the other two options it explored. But sale critics argue the deal contains loopholes that would allow Confluence to reap profits from the sale while failing to invest in the dams’ maintenance or eventual removal, ultimately leaving taxpayers to inherit vast costs and public safety risks should the dams fall into disarray. Some of them also question whether a sale is the cheapest option. For nearly a year, Consumers refused to budge as critics sought changes to the deal. The utility’s stance changed after an administrative law judge urged the Public Service Commission to reject the sale, calling it “highly problematic” and “inconsistent with the public interest.” Since its first extension request in September, utility officials have met repeatedly with sale opponents but shown little interest in making meaningful concessions, Nessel told Bridge. She said she remains opposed to the sale and doesn’t believe further settlement talks will be fruitful. “We know what happens when you have a private owner of critical infrastructure, and they decide they’re not making money anymore, and they stop proper maintenance of a dam,” Nessel said. “I don’t think we want to relive that.” Unless the parties file a settlement agreement or collectively ask for more time by Dec. 9, Scripps said, the commission will rule on the sale plan at its Dec. 17 meeting.

articles.title: A man named Chris will be New Zealand's next prime minister, whichever party wins the election
articles.description: A man named Chris will be New Zealand's next prime minister, whichever party wins the election AP News A moderate millennial newcomer could decide knife-edge New Zealand election CNN New Zealand election campaign enters final day with result too close to call Reuters The New Zealand Election That Could ‘Flip the Table’ The New York Times Gangs, gaffes and two guys named Chris: why I’m glued to the 2026 New Zealand el
articles.content: WELLINGTON, New Zealand (AP) — New Zealand is choosing a new government in a national election that concludes Saturday. But one outcome is already known: The next prime minister will be a man named Chris. The leaders of the nation’s two biggest political parties bear that name. Center-right National is helmed by Christopher Luxon, who has been prime minister since the 2023 election, when his party ousted center-left Labour, led by Chris Hipkins. Both leaders in the “battle of the Chrises” are, according to most opinion polls, fairly unpopular with voters. The ascension of political Chrises is linked to the popularity of the name Christopher for New Zealand children until the mid-1980s, peaking in 1968 when nearly 800 babies were given the name, according to government data. In 2025, just 20 newborns were named Christopher. Here’s how to tell the political leaders apart. The National party’s leader and incumbent prime minister, Luxon, 56, was one of more than 600 Christophers born in New Zealand in 1970. When he took power after the 2023 election, Luxon was a relative political novice who had first been elected to Parliament in 2020. Before entering politics he was head of national carrier Air New Zealand. He also worked in the United States and Canada as an executive for consumer packaged goods firm Unilever. Luxon, a father of two, has often declined to discuss his Christian faith publicly in resolutely secular New Zealand, a country where politicians who hold strong religious views are sometimes seen as suspect. His party was elected on his pledges of economic growth, and Luxon highlighted his own business acumen when he said he would seek deals abroad for New Zealand. Luxon says his achievements in office include a free trade deal negotiated and signed between New Zealand and India, export growth, education reforms and tougher measures against criminal gangs. His detractors note that domestic economic recovery has been slow, with living costs and unemployment stubbornly high. They portray Luxon, a millionaire, as disconnected from the struggles of ordinary people. In 2026 Luxon survived an unusual pair of confidence votes among his lawmakers over his leadership of the party, after slumps in opinion polling and verbal gaffes that some analysts said reflected his political inexperience. The National leader prompted one of the votes himself as speculation grew that he might be toppled by his party. The second vote followed a leadership bid from another Chris, then Defense Minister Chris Penk, who was sacked from the Cabinet by Luxon and will leave politics after the election. Transport Minister Chris Bishop, third-ranked in Luxon’s cabinet, is often mentioned as a possible successor for the party’s leadership. The Labour party’s leader, Hipkins, 48, was born in 1978 when he was one of more than 400 babies to receive the name Christopher. Hipkins became prime minister without a general election in January 2023 after his then-leader Jacinda Ardern abruptly quit, citing exhaustion following more than five years in the job. After nine months as prime minister, Hipkins led Labour to electoral defeat and became leader of the opposition. He began in politics as student body president at his university, where he studied political science, and entered New Zealand’s parliament in 2008 at age 30. The father of two was handed weighty portfolios in Ardern’s Cabinet, including health, education and responsibility for New Zealand’s pandemic response. While the public health outcomes of the country’s strict COVID-19 lockdowns were praised by experts globally, Labour faced a backlash against the economic impact of the measures on the biggest city, Auckland. Hipkins, who has campaigned in 2026 on pledges to curb steep living costs and boost funding for New Zealand’s public healthcare system, is still negatively associated with the pandemic-era policies by opponents. He presents himself as a relatable everyman. After Ardern announced she would quit, Hipkins spoke to reporters dressed in a hoodie, baseball cap and wraparound sunglasses, provoking memes on social media. His love of sausage rolls is so well-documented that he has been served them by foreign leaders on official visits abroad. During the pandemic, Hipkins made headlines when he told a news conference it was difficult for people to “get outside and spread their legs” without infecting others. He later clarified that he had intended to say “stretch their legs,” but the phrase went viral. No other lawmakers in his party are called Chris.

articles.title: Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets
articles.description: Software optimizes a physical model of the telescope to reduce noise.
articles.content: With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet. While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star's light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope's configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets. Point spreads Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.Read full article Comments

articles.content: Freedom Fuel stations have drawn in customers with cheap gas. A recent lawsuit claims the company hasn’t fully paid for the gas they sell. At the intersection Cadieux and Harper sits the Freedom Fuel gas station. The new chain of Freedom Fuel gas stations that emerged across the country this summer has opened two locations in Detroit. The first Freedom Fuel station opened in Philadelphia on July 7. On opening day, the price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.47 per gallon, almost 50 cents cheaper than the average gas station in Philly according to GasBuddy. President Trump endorsed the stations, saying they were taking the lead on selling affordable gas and others should follow. Detroit’s first Freedom Fuel station opened on Aug. 2, on Harper Ave. near Cadieux, offering gas at $3.47 per gallon. Records from GasBuddy put the average cost of gas in Detroit around that time at around $4.31 per gallon. A second location opened a month later on W. McNichols and Third Street. That station opened at $3.99 when the average cost of gas was around $4.07. The Detroit locations joined stations in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, bringing the number of Freedom Fuel stations to 30. In August oil supplier Mansfield Oil filed a lawsuit against one of the owners of the Freedom Fuel Network, KRSM in Pennsylvania. Mansfield says it never received payment for approximately 1.1 million gallons of fuel worth almost $4 million. Mansfield says KRSM sold a portion of that fuel at Freedom Fuel locations. KRSM is owned by brothers Syed and Shamikh Kazmi. It partially owns at least 14 of the stations. Eight stations are leased directly to Shamikh Kazmi from Blue Owl Capital. In court files, KRSM cited a data error as the reason Mansfield did not receive the information needed to send KRSM invoices. Mansfield says it corrected the error then sent the invoices back to KRSM. Mansfield says KRSM still has not paid. KRSM and the Freedom Fuel Network have not responded to a request for comment on the lawsuit and other information about the gas stations in Detroit. articles.description: Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) was named the next Senate majority leader by the Democratic caucus on Thursday afternoon. Talking to reporters after the vote, Camilleri repeatedly said that his […]
articles.content: Incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) and outgoing Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) speak on the Senate floor prior to caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) was named the next Senate majority leader by the Democratic caucus on Thursday afternoon. While he will not officially assume the role until voted in by the full chamber in January, his nomination by the Democrats makes that a formality. Talking to reporters after the vote, Camilleri repeatedly said that his goal is to ensure that the upcoming legislative session is “the most productive legislative session in our lifetimes.” He later went on to say that his metric for that was having the most “meaningful” bills signed into law. “My caucus was sent here with a mandate to lower the cost of living for our residents, to address the many problems that Michigan has not been able to address for the last two years, and get things done for working people,” he said. “We are incredibly excited at the chance for us to take on a big, bold agenda with our brand new Democratic trifecta, and be in a position to solve as many problems as we can.” Camilleri will assume the majority leader role with a 23-15 majority in the chamber — significantly larger than the last session, where Democrats held just a single seat majority for most of the term and did not control the House, and larger than the session prior, in which Democrats had a trifecta but only a two-seat margin in the Senate. State Senate Democrats take a selfie in the Senate chamber prior to caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) With such a large majority in the Senate, as well as a large Democratic majority in the House, Camilleri said, “Our goal will be to make sure that we can again do big bold things in this new trifecta. I can’t again give you a list today, but I do believe that because we have returned with stronger majorities than we’ve ever really had, we’ll have a chance to do a lot more.” A significant portion of the Democratic caucus is new to the state Senate, and many members are new to the Legislature completely. Camilleri said their wide breadth of experiences and backgrounds will help inform legislative priorities for the next two years, though some will have to get up to speed on the workings of the Legislature. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores), who was chosen by the Democrats as the next Majority Floor Leader, will play a role in that, Camilleri said. “We want to make sure with this diverse caucus that everybody, everybody’s ideas are on the table, that every voice is being heard, and that we are being extremely productive,” Hertel told reporters. “That’s the role of the floor leader to make sure everything’s moving in a smooth fashion. That the caucus is getting the information that they need.” Lt. Governor-elect and outgoing Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said she feels “great about the handoff” and emphasized the importance of having wide margins in both chambers of the legislature to help the executive leadership push through their agenda. Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson also expressed support for Camilleri’s leadership, telling reporters, “My ask of all of them was to be bold. Let’s take big swings together. Let’s transform our state. And the other thing I said was that I intend to be collaborative. I know they all have great ideas. They come here representing their communities with a vision for what they want to achieve. I want to have them achieve it.” Incoming Senate Minority Leader Roger Hauck (R-Mt. Pleasant) speaks to reporters following caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance) Republicans chose Sen. Roger Hauck (R-Mt. Pleasant) as their caucus leader. While some had speculated there might be a contentious leadership election in the minority, Hauck said his election was unanimous and that he “put that to rest.” “Obviously, we start out in a bad situation. We only have 15 members, right, and they have 23, so they’re not going to need us as much,” he told reporters after his selection. “But I promised the majority leader and Senator Hertel that I would work with them.” Republicans also announced their full leadership team in a press release. Sen. Thomas Albert (R-Lowell) will serve as Republican Floor Leader, Sen.-elect John Wetzel (R-Grand Haven) as Republican Whip, Sen.-elect Gina Johnsen (R-Portland) as Republican Caucus Chair, Sen. Michele Hoitenga (R-Manton) as Assistant Republican Leader, Sen.-elect Mike Murphy (R-Howell) as Assistant Republican Floor Leader, Sen.-elect Donni Steele (R-Orion Township) as Assistant Republican Whip, and Sen. Jonathan Lindsey (R-Coldwater) as Assistant Republican Caucus Chair.
