articles.title: Commentary: Healthcare workers must stand up to ICE
articles.description: Federal officials allege that on May 28th, 2026, a nurse at Trinity Health Ann Arbor helped a patient who had been detained and injured by ICE to escape custody. The state is now charging this nurse, Chloe Renee Freeman, with a federal misdemeanor. As ICE, DHS, and other arms of state violence increase their systematic […]
articles.content: A man identified only as 'OBP' in federal court records is pictured in surveillance footage as he leaves Trinity Health Ann Arbor on May 28, 2026. A nurse from the hospital, Chloe Renee Freeman, has been charged by authorities with "Instigating or Assisting Escape of Person Under Arrest, a misdemeanor offense." (Photo is a screenshot from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan)Federal officials allege that on May 28th, 2026, a nurse at Trinity Health Ann Arbor helped a patient who had been detained and injured by ICE to escape custody. The state is now charging this nurse, Chloe Renee Freeman, with a federal misdemeanor. As ICE, DHS, and other arms of state violence increase their systematic assault on immigrant communities, Freeman’s alleged actions exemplify what solidarity from the medical field can and should look like. Under the current ICE siege, hospitals have become battlegrounds. Immigration agents often brutalize their targets, then bring them to emergency departments on their way to detention centers. This means that hospitals are often the first point at which people are disappeared into ICE custody. Once inside the emergency room, agents use pseudonyms to obscure the location of detained migrants; they deny patients visits with their community or lawyers; they physically restrain and surveil migrants; they harass and threaten staff. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE These acts of violence are not only deeply immoral, they are also often illegal, violating migrant patients’ rights to care and to privacy. Once transported to detention centers, patients are subjected to severe medical neglect that can be life-threatening. They not only lack access to medication, medical professionals, disability accommodations, and other forms of treatment, but also lack clean air, food, water, adequate clothing, and access to hygiene. Temperatures are dangerous high or low, and raw sewage and dangerous insects abound; staff are physically and verbally violent. ICE detention is unsafe for anyone, much less patients who have been injured by ICE or who have any sort of illness, chronic condition, or disability. These concentration-camp-esque conditions have contributed to 52 deaths in ICE detention so far between January 2025 and June 2026. Healthcare workers have a moral and professional duty to protect our patients. Complicity in ICE’s kidnappings is a violation of our mandate to do no harm. Healthcare workers who take action in solidarity with detained migrants, as Freeman is alleged to have done, exemplify courage and moral clarity. These workers often act in defiance of a workplace culture which demands compliance with state violence and which capitulates to ICE, even when not legally required. But they are not alone. They are part of a rich history of healthcare workers declining to adhere to immoral laws, from doctors who participated in the Underground Railroad to underground abortion practitioners to healthcare workers providing gender affirming care despite criminalization. Today, resistance to ICE’s occupations of our hospitals and emergency rooms is everywhere. When healthcare workers are willing to take action in solidarity, hospitals can also be spaces where kidnapped migrants are reappeared. For example, in LA and St. Paul, medical staff connected detained migrants in their care to legal resources. They kept these patients in their respective hospitals, instead of releasing them into ICE custody. Attorneys were able to fight for these patients’ release from ICE custody, and in both cases they were returned to their communities without entering a detention center. Nessel praises ruling temporarily blocking Trump administration from sharing health data with ICE Organizing collectively can lead to even bigger wins, such as a May 2026 policy passed in L.A. to expand protections against ICE for hospital patients and staff. As healthcare workers, we stand with Chloe Renee Freeman, and with all care providers who are penalized for protecting their patients. Freeman’s experiences shed light on the broader failures of our healthcare and legal systems, which surveil patients, criminalize their care, and punish providers for protecting their patients. We call on the federal government to drop Freeman’s charges. We call on Michigan’s Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA) not to punish Freeman or anyone else accused of non-cooperation with ICE. And more broadly, we call on our fellow healthcare workers to stand in solidarity with our patients by working towards systemic change within medicine in the following ways: End police and ICE presence in and near healthcare facilities End medically unnecessary information gathering, documentation, and surveillance Stop calling police or ICE on patients Stop providing or sanctioning substandard and/or coercive care in prisons, jails, detention centers, and other facilities Stop punishing healthcare workers for refusal to participate in systems of harm We must resist turning our hospitals and clinics into prisons, our nurses into jailors. If you are a healthcare worker, there are several ways to get involved supporting Chloe Freeman and fighting for immigrants. You can support Chloe by signing our letter of support here. Or get involved with your local ICE rapid response group – many immigrant rights organizations have connections with various local rapid response networks. If you want to work specifically within the medical system, Beyond Do No Harm is a group of healthcare workers working to interrupt criminalization in southeastern Michigan; you can contact them here.

articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. An SRT file (SubRip Subtitle file) is a plain text file that stores subtitles as numbered blocks, with each block pairing a start and end timestamp with the caption text that appears on screen between them. Millions of people watch videos with the sound off every day. Verizon was one of the first companies to report on this behavior in 2019, when it found that 69% of polled users in the U.S. turned the sound off on videos in public spaces. It also found that 80% of consumers were more likely to watch an entire video when it had captions. A 2024 study cited these findings from Verizon and confirmed that they still hold true. It’s no wonder that both individual content creators and big media teams prioritize captions on everything from social media videos to ads and movies. You can use ElevenCreative to produce studio-grade audio, automate caption workflows, and add subtitles to a video in seconds. This not only boosts engagement but also makes videos more accessible for people who are hard of hearing or deaf and people who speak different languages. This guide shows you how to use the SRT file format to create, edit, and add subtitles to your videos. You’ll also see how the SRT file format works, learn how to open the format on any device, and figure out when to choose between SRT and WebVTT. A SubRip Subtitle (SRT) file is a plain-text subtitle format that pairs blocks of text with start and end timestamps. This lightweight file tells a video player exactly what captions to display on screen and when. Creators and media teams use the SRT file format to add subtitles to videos distributed across publishing channels. The SRT file format is widely supported and works independently of any single proprietary tool. As a direct result of this, most tools open and parse these files easily. Major streaming platforms and media players also have the built-in ability to process them. This makes it easy to add subtitles to your videos without getting locked into proprietary software. The SRT file format structures subtitle tracks into a clean sequence of numbered blocks. Each block contains three core components that control how captions sync with video playback. A single blank line separates each subtitle entry from the next block in the file. A numbered index opens each block to define its order in the timeline. Underneath this index, a timestamp line specifies the precise start and end times for displaying the corresponding text. The plain text caption appears directly under the timecode line before a blank line marks the end of that block. Reviewing a real example of two formatted blocks clarifies how sequence numbers, timestamps, and text blocks align within an SRT file: Welcome to another adventure in the forgotten villages of rural Spain. Every village has its unique traditions that have barely changed in hundreds of years. The blank line between the two blocks marks where one caption ends and the next begins. The timestamp line requires exact formatting in the HH:MM:SS,mmm structure. Format hours (HH), minutes (MM), and seconds (SS), separated by colons, and then a comma before the milliseconds (mmm). Failing to follow this format is a common source of captioning errors. Most video players and editing software have native support for opening the SRT file format, eliminating the need for extra plugins. Follow these steps to open SRT files in most text editing or video playback tools across just about any device: A TXT to SRT converter adds start and end timestamps to plain text and turns it into numbered subtitle blocks that a video player can display. A plain text file has no timing information, which means the timestamps have to come from the audio itself. ElevenCreative uses an automated speech to text workflow to generate them. Plain text on its own has no timing, which means the conversion depends on where the timestamps come from. If you already have a transcript, you can type the timecodes into each block by hand, which works for short clips. For anything longer, run the original recording through speech to text and let the model generate the words and timestamps together. Here’s how to generate and export your SRT file from the transcript of your video or recording: Creators can also access the no-code export path on the speech to text playground to convert transcripts directly in the browser. Learning how to edit subtitle files keeps your video captions synchronized with spoken dialogue. Creators with this skill can modify text lines, adjust timestamps, and refine line lengths directly using just the plain text file or browser-based subtitling tools. Subtitle tracks often have noticeable timing and readability errors. Knowing the most common errors can help you catch them before they become a post-production nightmare. The editing process is a simple final step for polishing your recording for publishing. You can use the following steps to get started: For longer videos, a dedicated SRT editor makes timing fixes faster. It shows the video preview next to the timecodes, which lets you spot drift and overlaps as you edit. Attaching an SRT file to your video project is also a simple process. Choose one of these three options, depending on where the video will be shown: Choosing the right subtitle file format comes down to where you publish your video content. An SRT file is the most widely supported format, so it’s still used across desktop players, legacy media platforms, and offline editing applications. Its plain-text structure gives content creators maximum compatibility without the need for specialized software to load or preview text files. However, WebVTT is the newer web standard designed specifically for HTML5 web video players. Unlike the basic SRT file format, WebVTT supports additional features like advanced text styling, font colors, and custom screen positioning. These features make it a better choice for web-first video distribution and HTML5 web players where positioning and visuals matter. ElevenCreative supports both subtitle export options directly from our speech to text transcription workflow. You automatically generate your timed transcript and export it as an SRT or WebVTT file in seconds. This makes it easy to pick the file format that best matches your target player, audience, or use case. Developers and engineers use ElevenAPI to automate subtitle generation across high-volume video workflows. The ElevenLabs Scribe v2 model transcribes audio in over 90 languages and delivers word-level timestamps directly into your app. The system instantly converts spoken audio into structured captions, which eliminates manual data entry. Automating subtitle pipelines speeds up media distribution, especially for time-sensitive content. It also ensures precise timecode synchronization for a professional and accurate finish across worldwide platforms. Read our speech to text cookbook to view code samples and start building your subtitle pipeline. You can also generate an API key in your developer dashboard to add subtitles to a video at scale. Alternatively, sign up for ElevenCreative to use the subtitle generator today. Generate an API to start generating subtitles at scale The SRT extension (.srt) marks a SubRip text file that stores plain text captions and their start and end timestamps. Creators use this file format across video platforms to add subtitles without advanced features like custom placement and visual style. ElevenCreative also provides a no-code speech to text workspace that automatically generates exported SRT file tracks from your audio or video recordings. You can open it in any text editor, such as Notepad or TextEdit, to read or change the text and timecodes. Most video players can also load it alongside a video file to display the subtitles. There are three ways to create an SRT file. You can write it by hand in a text editor using the numbered block format, which gets slow for longer videos. You can use a subtitle editor to type captions against a video preview. Or you can generate it automatically by uploading your audio or video to a speech to text tool such as ElevenCreative, reviewing the timed transcript, and exporting it as SRT. To get an MP4 with subtitles, add the SRT file to your video in a video editor and export the project as MP4 with the captions burned in. This renders the text permanently into the footage. If you want viewers to turn captions on and off, keep the SRT as a separate file or upload it to your publishing platform instead. An SRT editor is a subtitle tool that shows each caption’s text and timecodes next to a video preview. Unlike a plain text editor, it lets you adjust timing visually and can flag problems such as overlapping timestamps. Choose one when you are editing many captions or need to fix timing drift across a whole video. Queer Michigan history was made in the midterms this year
articles.description: As Democrats nationwide and across Michigan celebrated historic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, history was also made by a number of LGBTQ+ Michiganders. Among them was state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield), who was elected to the state’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the first openly gay member of Congress from Michigan. Joanna Whaley also made […]
articles.content: LGBTQ+ flags fly at the Michigan Capitol near the state Senate building during Michigan Pride in Lansing on June 26, 2022. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)As Democrats nationwide and across Michigan celebrated historic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, history was also made by a number of LGBTQ+ Michiganders. Among them was state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield), who was elected to the state’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the first openly gay member of Congress from Michigan. Joanna Whaley also made history, becoming Michigan’s first openly transgender state legislator when she was elected to Michigan’s 2nd House District. “I’ve always said, you can’t be what you can’t see,” Moss said in an interview with Michigan Advance. “I think it’s important for all of us to be in the rooms where decisions about us are being made, and again, I’m a representative from my neighborhood. I’m a representative from my community. I’m a representative from my district, and I also happen to be gay,” he continued. “I’m shaped by everything that my neighbors are shaped by. But I also have a story to tell about how policy decisions impact LGBTQ people, and that’s the important dynamic here. We’re just as ingrained in Michigan as anybody else is.” Senate Regulatory Affairs Committee Chair Jeremy Moss (D-Southfield) hears testimony on a bill cutting back on incoming changes to Michigan’s earned sick time law during a Feb. 11, 2025 meeting. | Kyle Davidson Whaley similarly said that she believes that when people — including transgender folks in Michigan looking to her — see someone like themselves in government, it will inspire them to believe that they, too, can lead. “We do that by leading with competence and using our skills, not because of who we are, but because we want to serve,” Whaley said. “And if they feel like their government is going after them and attacking them, then that’s their call to be in the room.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Whaley faced a campaign eligibility complaint during the primary from her Democratic opponent, Frank Liberati, and again faced transphobic attacks in the general election cycle from Republican Ron Kokinda, who she defeated by a 24-point margin on Tuesday. Whaley and her campaign — which was not focused on her transgender identity, but on affordability and accountability for her Downriver district — were able to overcome those types of attacks twice, which Whaley said makes her believe that the messaging attacking her for her gender identity did not resonate with voters, in her district or elsewhere nationwide. “I think our community and the state in general has finally said we reject culture war crap. They want politicians who are going to do the work and show up for them,” Whaley said. “This election cycle, from the U.S. Senate down into our race, were some of the most vile, disgusting political attacks I think I’ve ever seen in my lifetime. I am really proud of our community for sifting through the junk and listening for the substance.” State Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley, who will be representing Michigan’s 2nd House District after winning in Tuesday’s election. (Photo courtesy of Joanna Whaley) Moss, who was the first openly gay member of the Michigan Senate and one of the first openly gay members of the Legislature, said that Whaley’s election is important because, while he has worked hard to advocate for trans Michiganders and their needs, he is not part of that community. As anti-trans attacks and rhetoric escalate nationwide, “for the very first time in the Michigan legislature, every piece of the community has representation,” he said. Moss also shared a similar sentiment to Whaley about how much Michiganders actually care about culture war issues like transgender girls participating in sports. “I really, truly don’t know any family in this district that sits at the dinner table lamenting about a trans athlete. I don’t,” he said. “They do lament over the grocery bills. They do lament about gas prices. They do lament about access to healthcare should they need it. That’s what real people are talking about. So, I’d love to cut through the chaos of Trump’s administration and really deliver for people back home.” Moss and Whaley are not alone in making history for queer Michiganders in government. State Rep. Jason Hoskins (D-Southfield), who was elected to fill Moss’s now-vacant seat in the state Senate, becomes the first openly gay Black member of the Michigan Senate, having previously been the first out person of color elected to the Michigan Legislature while serving in the state House. State Rep. Jason Hoskins (D-Southfield), speaking at a Lansing press conference to announce the reintroduction of the Michigan Voting Rights Act. May 19, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance “That’s another segment of our community that needs a voice, that needs representation. So everybody is bringing their unique experiences even from within the community to be able to make sure all of our challenges are being addressed,” Moss said of passing the baton to Hoskins. Joseph McClusky, who was elected to Michigan’s 86th House District on the west side of the state, is the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent that district — flipping it blue after being held by Rep. Nancy DeBoer (R-Holland), who as a city council member in Holland voted against anti-discrimination laws protecting LGBTQ+ people. And other LGBTQ+ state representatives, both new and incumbents, saw success on Tuesday — Pride Source reported that every LGBTQ+ incumbent in the Michigan Legislature won their reelection campaign. Chris Gilmer-Hill, Mike McFall, Laurie Pohutsky, Noah Arbit, Jason Morgan and Emily Dievendorf will all serve in the Michigan House of Representatives as openly LGBTQ+ members, bringing the total number of openly LGBTQ+ state legislators in Michigan to nine.

articles.title: Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe first drive: Where tech and fun collide
articles.description: The spirit of AMG is alive via three axial flux electric motors.
articles.content: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from San Francisco to Malaga, Spain, and accommodation so Ars could drive the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. The night before I drove the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, I complained to a group of journalists that automakers don't want to take chances and just build fun, weird cars anymore. About 12 hours later, Mercedes made me eat my words. Outside of all the bombastic extravaganza of the Los Angeles launch, the first true AMG powered exclusively by batteries is a technological triumph that's as comfortable on the track as it is on the street. And it's really very good on the track. Triforce One of the fundamental problems with EVs is weight. Batteries are heavy, and the old rule about an object in motion tending to stay in motion makes the notion of nimble cornering a difficult engineering problem. Mercedes loves an engineering problem, and after two days behind the wheel of the AMG GT EV, the company has mostly reduced the battery-weight tax that mires EV performance. On the road and on the track, the vehicle is firmly planted to the roadway. Mercedes says various technologies make this possible. In addition to decades of producing high-performance vehicles, the automaker's AMG.EA sports-car architecture does a lot of heavy lifting here, constantly adjusting power delivery from the three motors while guiding the Active Ride Control suspension, steering—including up to 6 degrees at the rear axle—and active aerodynamics to deliver the performance AMG customers have come to expect from a vehicle with the Affalterbach badge on the hood.Read full article Comments

articles.title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
articles.description: Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, OpenAI’s cybersecurity model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within authorized scope.
articles.content: A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set. We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox. On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately. These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities(opens in a new window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure. It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber. GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra. Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings. One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement. We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card(opens in a new window) for full results. One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task. GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time. We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds: GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review: We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors. Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years: Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports(opens in a new window). Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed. Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli(opens in a new window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications. As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization. We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card(opens in a new window) for full information): Cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing. Targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems. Private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel. Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise. Sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing(opens in a new window), action review(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows. Protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more). Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks. First, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a new group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment. Second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber. Higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%. To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions. We used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. articles.title: Launch of EU-GAINS website
articles.source: IARC – INTERNATIONAL AGENCY FOR RESEARCH ON CANCER
articles.content: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) today launched a new project website for the European Guidelines and Quality Assurance on Primary Prevention of Gastric Cancer and the Third European Union (EU) Cancer Screening Report (EU-GAINS) project. The website outlines the goals of the project, introduces the partners, describes the work packages and methods designed to achieve these goals, and provides context for the research in relation to previous efforts and the burden of gastric cancer. Information related to Working Group meetings and publications resulting from the work will also be made available on the website. The overall objective of EU-GAINS is to develop the first evidence-based European guidelines for population-based Helicobacter pylori screen-and-treat programmes for the European Commission Initiative on Gastric Cancer (EC-GaC), as the primary strategy for preventing gastric cancer, while paving the way for development of the quality assurance scheme for the strategy. EU-GAINS will also produce the Third EU Cancer Screening Report, providing an updated overview of the implementation of cancer screening across Europe. The project’s outcomes will strengthen cancer prevention and screening in Europe and bolster coordination of these efforts, thereby contributing to the implementation of the new EU Cancer Screening Scheme, which is one of the flagship initiatives of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. EU-GAINS is a 2-year project led by IARC in close collaboration with the EC Joint Research Centre (JRC). The project is co-funded by the EU.
